PHILANTHROPY : "You look a broken-down man. Hard work do it?" Seedy: "No ; looking for work." . "Do you sing to your baby to quiet him!" " Yee ; but sometimes I think he goes to sleep to quiet me." Asszsca makes the heart grow fonder. The schoolboy loves his dear teacher most during vaca- tion time. SHE "It requires money to get into society nowadays." He: " Yes ; and it requires brains to keep out of it." " WHAT a dream of a bonnet she has on !" " Yes ; and to keep the balance even her husband wears a wide-awake." CHANGED. —" They say her parents are common." "Not at all. But I understand they were so before they got their money."
• AMATEUR, PHOTOGRAPHY.—Daughter : "Where have sister and George gone?" Father: " I've sent them into the dark room to develop their affections."
ITS FATlL—Wheeler : "Heavens I That bicycle brigade has been utterly destroyed !" Biker: "Horrors I The enemy?" Wheeler: "No. Some fool started a discussion as to the best make." .

INDICATIONS Ol IT.—Beth (near a hive, hearing the bees buzzing): "Gracious ! they must be making lots of honey, I should think, by their gra nding." No A SVCCESS.—Bauer: "I understand that the speaker made a poor impression." Wheat : " Yes ; he spent five minutes clearing his throat and twenty minutes clearing the hall." HOPB.—Brown : "Can the doctor cure your insomnia?" Jones: " Yes ; he thinks I'll soon be able to sleep it off." THE ItzssoN WHY. —" Why does that dog of Jackson's take such a delight in biting little children!" "He was brought up on infant food, you know." MAMMA: "I'm surprised at you, Johnny !" Johnny (thoughtfully) : "I wonder if you'll ever get used to me, mamma? You're always surprised at me." "THE gentlemen that came to see papa said I was one of the most intelligent children they ever saw," said little Jai*. "Indeed," said the proud mothar. "Did you recite little Drops of Water' for them?" "No'in. I refused to." PATSY WHALEN (studying his lessen): "Sir Is.itte Newton discovered the great law of gravita- tion by an apple falling on his head." Whalen: "Soure, an it's a good t ing for science thot it wasn't a hod o' bricks, thin, or he'd never knowed phwat it was." MRS. SPRINGS: "How careful your little boy is of his health! My boy is constantly running out in all sorts ox weather, without overcoat or overs!-:oe, no matter what I say. How do you manage?" Mrs. Briggs: "When my boy catches cold I give him cod liver Oil." WALKER: "You know the saying, Let me make the songs of a nation and I don't care woo makes its laws!'" i, Fraser: "Yes. What about it?" Walker: "It ought to read, Let me make the laws of a nation and I'll put in gaol half the folks who make its songs.'" Mits. BINKS : "My husband did not like that tea you sent us last." Grocer (politely): " Did you like it, madam?" Mrs. Binks : "Yes ; I liked it." Grocer (to clerk): "James, send Mr. Blake another pound of the same tea as she had last. Anything else, madam?"

IN the early part of the Queen's reign a story Was current that her Majesty once asked the Duke of Wellington what kind of boots he was in the habit of wearkg. "People call them Wellingtor,4, ma'am," he answered. "How absurd I" Her Majesty exclaimed. "Where, I should like to know, would they find a pair of Wellingtons?" Mae. Wordswith (sharply concluding the sentence): "Mouse !" Mrs. Wordswith (forgetting the thread of her discourse in the agitation of the moment): " Where ? Oh, George, o protect me " AN UNHAPPY COUPLE.. —Martha : "Helen and Harry act as though they were heartily sick of one another, and they haven't been married more than a year." Bertha: "Well, I don't wonder. Not long ago they took to reading the love letters they wrote when they were courting. "Of course after ttot, it was impossible for either to have much respect for the other."

- STILL ANOTHER Psoutins.—" They have now invented an electric key-hole," she said, pointedly. "An electric key-hole l' he repeated, in a puzzled tone. "Yes," she answered, "an electric key- hole. When a man comes home late at night al I he has to do is to touch a button and a light shines out, showing him exactly where the key-hole Li." "I will admit," he said, thoughtfully, "than that solves one problem, but how is the man who comes home late at night to find the button?"

Tnain RAPID TRANSIT. —Hand in hand they strolled in the quiet evening, happy in themselveß and their surroundings. Suddenly the girl halted and said: "Percy, what is that?" Percy, without releasing her hand, stopped, and said: "Gladys darling, it's a snail." And so they wandered on for a sweet half-hour longer, when the maiden again said: Percy, look, there's Another snail." Percy again bent his manly form, and looking up replied: "No, Glayds, 'tis the same snail."

Well, there was no sleep for me the nig:, -!!!be peat day the old woman cut up so rough fgot scared, end, thinking to divert any po,vibl.. A CURE FOR BALKING. —I was riding along a mountain road in East Kentucky (writes a ravel. ler), when I saw a mule running towards me with a singletree dangling at his heels. With great difficulty I got out of his way. About a mile jar. ther on I saw two front wheels and the waggon box. I looked round to see if the driver had been hurt; but, finding no one, I drove on. In a few minutes I met a man walking rather quickly dovi n the road. "Stranger," he asked, "did you see a mule down that road?" "Yes." "Did he hey a rag over his ear?" "I didn't see any." " Waal, it's all right. I reckon 'e'll stop when 'e gets flustered out, an' I reckon 'e's cured." "What is he cured of?" I asked. " Balkin'. You see, I heerd that a grasshopper put in th' ear o' a hose or mule 'd cure 'an from balkin'. So I tied a rag over the critter's ear so it couldn't get out, cotched a grasshopper, put 'im in, an', stranger, it's the Lest remedy I ever seed. Th' mule dian't give me no time to get in th' waggon. I never seed a mule so sprightly. I reckon th' hopper's got out now, an' ru go and cotch the mule." A Goon DOG.—Fair Customer: "I live in the suburbs, and I want a good house-dog." Dealer: "Yes, mum." "But, of course, I don't want one that will keep us awake all night barking at nothing." "No, mum." "He must be big and strong and fierce, you know. "Yes, mum." "Yet as gentle as a lamb with us, you know." yes, mum." "And he must pounce on every tramp that comes along and drive him off." "Yes, mum." 'But he mustn't interfere with any poor but honest man looking for work." "No, mum." "If a burglar comes prowling about at tsnt the dog should make mincemeat of him in an instant." "Yes, mum." "But he mustn't attack a neighbour who drops in for an evening call." "No, mum." "And, of course, he mustn't molest people who come hurrying in at all hours of the night to call, my husband. He's the doctor, you know." "No, mum. I see what you want. You want a thought-reader dog." "Yes, I sup- pose so." "Very sorry, mum, but I'm out of that kind of dog."

Dzea NELLIE, I notice that the hat described as " lamp-shade " because it is comp/peed of innumerable frills of chiffon and lace hat re-appeared this season, but it will not be the most fashionable type of head- gear for smart functions. Rig Leghorn hats with very flat crowns and drooping brims are in high favour, as are similar shapes in Cuban straw, the trimming consisting of a large wreath of flowers laid on the brim, and a bow of black velvet at the back. A few hats of stitched linen have been brought out, but they are not popular. A charm- hg bat is in pale blue straw, with marguerites massed at the back, together with a black velvet bow; black velvet loops also nestle bet,veen the folded-over brim in front. Another hat is a double plateau of white chip, stitched with black. Black velvet passes across the crown and falls on the hair behind, and a large Marechal Niel rose with foliage is poised in front. Underneath is a good example of the visite, made in cream alpaca, with ,soante linen lace collar and cuffs, and black velvet -rosettes down the front. Round the front is a Elk ruching. The hat, with its waved brim turned 'Off the face, has a bandeau of roses underneath. and is bound with black velvet.

The adaptation of old-fashioned collars and eevos is occasionally rather a puzzle. Very often the large collars are wrongly shaped for wear with the present style of bodice, but if they cannot be altered sufficiently to utilise as collars, they can often been made into pretty jabots if they are adroitly pleated or gathered and sewn to a ribbon er folded silk neckband. The smaller of tii( lit- fashioned undersleeves can be used wit'u the modern bell-shaped ones without altering, but the large open undersleeves are unsuitable. A pair of these sleeves, however, opened out, joioul together to make one fiat piece, and shaped a little, will form a nice fichu to drape a silk bodice, while an odd sleeve, if such a thing is among the stock.-will tarnish the material for tie ends. The small all- sound crochet collars look best mounted on deep- coloured cr black ribbon, or, if not liked for neck- wear, they can be utilised to border the rounded ends of large net scarves. Fin -11 y, let me say that old lace handkerchiefs, if nicely got-up, can be con- verted into quite smart fronts or jalots by doubling them from corner to corner diagonally, but un- equally, so that two corners show fully, and care- fully pleating the folded part to a ribbon band. 41. pin here and there will be neces.,ary to keep bhe front in effective folds when put on but f these are pretty, fanciful lace pits they need not be concealed.

r;veryoue knows how on really hot days gowns of foulard are much appreciated, but cheaper 'materials such as fonlardines and "mercerised &steeps make up well, and are quite as cool. Tnese Dew fabrics are almost indistinguishable from real foulards in appearance, although they do not, (4 course, wear so satisfactorily. A very pretty way of making up either a foulard or one of its imita- tions is as follows :—The skirt is bordered witk several narrow tucks, and a little distance above these are two narrow bands (or one broader one) of cream or ivory lace-insertion laid over plain. coloured sateen, or, in the case of a real foulard, of glace. The bodice has a smail square yoke of the lined lace, from which bands of the same are carried down to the waiat in front, and the sleeves are trimmed to match. A lilac and white foulard, for instance, might be trimmed with ivory lace and lilac silk, the belt being of deep lilac velvet with a handsome silver clasp. and the same idea coui.l Aioely carried out in shades of Wedgwood Floral uivalins are Likely to be extreakelyiasiii,.:l- -

able for garden pal ty awl fate gowns, and are to be had in the most charmink{ enlom-s and patterns. They are often made up in ultra-elaborate style, but they look nearly as well if quite a simple way is chosen, the skirt being edged with two or three flounces, and the full 'bodice draped about the shoulders with a lace-edged muslin fiehu and open- ing at the throat to show a little transparent shemisette of lace.

r Little Print* Edward of York his just enterel upon his eighth year, and on July 11.. h the Date and Duchess will celebrate the eighth anniversary of their wedding lay. —Since tbeir royal Highnesses left for their colonial ton?, thelEing and Queen have taken the most assiduous care of the royal children, giving the elder ones every possible kind of treat likely to amuse them, and on several occasions Queen Alexandra has been ,een driving with one of the younger children on her knee. ' At present more attention is being given to what may be called the outdoor training of Prince Edward and Prince Albert, but they have a few short school lessons from fildlie Brica, a great friend of the late Duchess of Teck. It is early yet to talk of a career for the little Princes of York,- but "allprobability they will take to the sea, and in due course join the •• Britannia." The arrival of yet another daughter must have been a keen disappointment to that illustrious couple' the Gear and Czarina. Unfortunately the latter has failed to win a very large place in the hearts of her husband's people, and the non-appearance, as yet, of a son and heir to the throne, has not m.de things better. Of the four daughters of the late Princess Alice, the Grand 'Duchess Serene is undoubtedly the most beautiful. The Catrina. too, is very Lively of course, tut her expression Is not so annabla or pleasing as that of her elder sister.

Battle Abbey which pass to Captain Forester after the death of the Ducbees of Cleveland, seems likely to once mote oonie late the market. The Property passed from one to another before It was acquired by the late Duke of Cleveland, and there is nothing to prevent its being bought and sold again. Still one would think Ithat the place, so full of historic memories, the scene of Harold's death, and the Norman victory, ought to be -secured for the nation, aod not left, perhaps, to be made ducks and drakes of, by some American millionaire or other latter-day plutocrat. If the property is to be sold, one would like to hear of its purchase by Lord Rose- bery, or some other nobleman, in whcse hands its fine Old ruins, which are so intimately associated with our history, would be safe from desecration. The Dowager Duchess of Abercorn, whose time is mostly spent at Coates Castle near Petworth, has re- cently been on a visit to London. This venerable lady will enter upon her ninetieth year on the Sth of July, and she can boast almost a record in the number of her descendants, of whom there are 130 a"; present living. She is a daughter of the sixth Duke of Bedford, and is the grand aunt of Earl Russell. whose matrimonial affairs have so often been the subject of legal proceed- ings. Earl Russell, is of ceurse, the grandson of Lord John Russell, but though hi-, voice has been beard once or twice in the House of le-3rds, he has not the oratorial or literary gifts rf his famous grsnefather. With the holidays in view, a bathing gown is, with the majority of us, almost a necessity. The best gar- ments are those made at home,or at least under personal superintendence. Properly shrunk serge should be used and ingrain braids and cottons, and in making up still further shrinkage ntust be allowed for in all the materials. At foreign watering places, dresses for the baths are a serious matter, and though we need not Icopy the extreme attire of some bathers, the dainty and eomfortable styles of others shame our conventional, and often ugly garments. Woollen materials are the most generally comfortable and suitable, and blue, ee3rlet and white prove the best colours. A bathing costume should be made in two pieces, rather fun knickerbockers and a deep Norfolk jacket, (the latter scalloped or vandyked round the edge), with a sailer collar. All embroidering and braiding on collar,belt and knee bands, must be flat, as fluttering ends are a nuis- ance. Altogether the home-worker has plenty of scope for ingenuity in planning these dresses. Waistbands are now as wide as they were formerly, usually narrow. The newfst are regular swathes of ribbon or soft silk, folied round and brought high up at the back, half-way up to the neck. There (if this eccentric mode must be followed) thee should be invisi- bly secured, but some make the foolish mistake of fastening them with a large and conspicuous buckle. Chise silks, with delicately colored designs make the prettiest waist belts, but need careful building, to in- duce them to take the required slope without an undue strain. It is wise to copy from a professional model and not to repeat this too often, as, in this extreme width, belts are not likely to last long in favour. After all there is nothing more useful than Petersham fastened with a realle handsome clasp. Wide soft sashes of silk are often seen over light dresses, but so draped as not to cover the fastenings at the waist, so they are decora- tive only, and for use we mnat still keep to belts of diverse forrr. S. . Some of the latest hats from l'atis suggest confection- ery. The straw looks cake-like in color and consistency, and is woven into large'circles. These are doubled and arranged on the head with the fold at the back, the gaping " oyster" opening along the front, being filled In with a half wreath of roses, primulas, forget-me-nots, or other small flowers. Through the double crown run two or more hat pins, and these, with perhaps a yard or two of the inevitable black velvet ribbon, complete an arrangement, which, to be fully apprecieed, must be seen from above. Baby bats, with huge floppy brims gathered round a low crown are popular with grown- ups. They certainly give plenty of shade, and in Idelicate colors are becoming to a young and pretty tone. In black they are too heavy-looking, while eerie, blue and white need courage, and are but too apt to be 1 favoured by those whoselcomplezions auffer cruelly from the Contact. Large etellete of lace and embroidery a e as much worn as ever, but now the extreme cheapness of Not. tingham and of imitation crochet laces has caused novelties to be introduced for these who can pay for them. The new mousseline app'iqui in the form of conventional leaves, makes pretty trimmings for bodices millinery and sunshades. These lace-like sprays in shape somewhat suggrst ti • ordinary silk artificial foliage, but are not so stiff. They are tacked together. and by the centres only, down to a muslin foundation the edges of the leaves curling about quite freely. Sometimes they cover the entire fichnen other instances they are laid upon mousseline de sole, or moth silk can- vas, which is allowed to show between them. Where this is the case, many mixtures of colors are possible, but for satisfactory effect there is nothing better than a black, white, or cream ground, for these white and ecru lace appliques. There was a time when to have red hair was eon• sidered a greet misfortune, but fashion has changed all that. Instead of dyeing it, or endeavouring to make it ruddr brown. every woman with red hair is now in- clined to make it as conspicuous as possible. Those so favoured have also the Rddittonal satisfaction of know- ing that they are not likely to go out of their mind. Nearly all mad people are dark-haired and dark skinned. and the idea that associates the red-headed with violence of mind, is it seems, quite a popular delusion. " MADGE."

fly 17LYSS ROGERSt Authi; of "For Love and the Queen," "Wedded in Mystery," dr.c.
CHAPTER XXXII, WHO FIRED THE SHOTS?
The news which had utterly unnerved and prostrated Grace Hendon was as follows: "The recent escape from Smilehurst. "Tragic fate of the runaway murderer.
"For a week the Smileburst officials have bees

scouring the countryside for the missing coniTICT Fenwick, the Fenwick murderer. It was not until last night, however, that any tidings had been gathered of him. About half-past seven a fisher- man at Bernard Bay, about four miles from Smile- hurst, noticed an object in the water, and upon approaching it found it to be the body of a man in convict's dress. It proved to be the missing prisoner. The body was greatly decomposed, but the dress with the convict's number, 35,' was intact.
"Upon getting the body ashore and making an official examination a strange discovery was made. The convict had been shot in the back. Medical

evidence is inclined, so it is stated, to the belief that the deceased met his death by drowning, and that the bullet wound was not in itself sufficient to cause death. The warders assert that, although the usual warning gun was fired over prisoner's head when he first bolted, they did not fire a single shot subsequently, the prisoner escaping so well into the gloom of the Smilehurst Forest that it would have been useless to fire. Others, how- ever, awr that they distinctly heard three shots fired. Doubtless this matter will be cleared up at the inquest, which will be held to-day. It seems strange that a man, after escaping the penalty of an awful crime, should meet his fate by sudden death in this way. The whole neighbourhood of Smilehurst has been in a state of terror since the escape of the prisoner." But the inquest throw no additional light upon the affair. The coroner had but one opinion upon the matter, which was that Samuels had shot ths runaway accidently, intending to fire over his head, that, weakened by the wound, the convict had not strength to manage the boat and had fainted and fallen overboard. But Samuels held to his assertion that he had not shot the prisoner, and some of the convicts is his gang, whose word, however, was not relied upon, testified to Samuels's side of the matter. Who had fired the two other shots that had been heard? The coroner explained the shots away as echoes from the depths of the forest; but the witnesses who heard them were positive, and equally positive were the other warders that they had not fired a single shot. The prisoner had cleared out too quickly to give them a chance. Someone started the theory that they had been fired in self-defence by some stranger who had been attacked by the convict. But in that case the shot would, in all probability, have been fired from the front and not from the back as it was quite evident this one was. Again, in such an event the man attacked would undoubtedly have made his tale known to the authorities. The whole thing, in fact, was an inscrutable mystery. Even Samuels, though he could have accounted for the boat or any other aid to the convict, found it utterly impossible to suggest to himself any feasible reason for the runaway being shot. "it is the strangest case I ever had before me," said the coroner. "I can suggest no other verdict to you than found dead,' gentlemen." "Found dead," therefore, was the verdict recorded. But the twelve good men and true went away scratching their heads in doubt, and the reporters left full of theories and solutions. "It was a mighty good job he never killed any- body," said the foreman over his glass of ale in the deputy-governor's room. It was an ambiguous though unconsciously true statement. "For my part I didn't feel safe whilst I knew he was loose and hereabouts. A man like him would have thought nothing cutting a throat or two to make good his escape.* "Aye, it's a mercy there's no harm done," said another. "There ought to be more care taken of them reprieved murderers. They ain't half-watch- ful enough of them, that's my opinion." As the coroner, after duly packing up the signed depositions and drinking a glass of wine with the governor, left the prison he almost ran down a 'deeply veiled young woman who was standing timidly on the steps of the room in which the court had been held. "A thousand pardons," he cried. Then he noticed that the face behind the veil was very white and drawn. He had seen many such faces about his courts. "You have come in reference to the inquest?" he said. "Is there anything I can do for you?" "Yes," she said; "I wish to see him." "Let me advise you as a friend not to do so. Unfortunately the body has been in the water a long time, and—you will say that it is kind of me afterwards. Remember him as you last saw him." He guessed instinctively that she was the lover or wife of the man. The coroner wondered that. such men could inspire love that would last through a prison career. Grace Hendon's grief had settled down to a calm melancholy, such melancholy as is often a prelude to madness. She listened t 9 the kindly words of the coroner as one stupefied and dazed. "Perhaps it would be beft ,r," she said, when he had finished. "When is the funeral ?"

"To-morrow," he . answered. "You aye staying in the town, perhaps. Let me give you a lift back.' She alcepted in quiet, lifeless tones, and together they back to the old market town. The coroner tried again and again to lift her out of herself by entern g into conversation, but Grace had httle to say besides the monosyllabic "yea" or She left him ether own request at the market- square, and went and made arrangements to stay the night at a quiet temperance hotel. .She had but a pound in her possession, and she spent several shillings in buying flowers to put on Martin's grave on the morrow. The next day she was up early, and an hour before the time fixed for the funeral made her way over the mile and a-half of dusty road to Smile- burst. When at length the convict procession started for the burial ground she followed and stood, with breaking heart but eyes from which no tears could force their way, listening to the cold, metallic voice of the chaplain as he read the service over the dead man and convicted lawbreaker.

The service over, Grace took a long, lasting look at the coffin, and for the first time a cry of anguish burst from her wounded soul. Then she dropped her flowers lightly upon the coffin and turned away. As she did so a man stepped up to her side. "Grace.'" She looked up. The dark eyes of Douglas Low were fired on hers.
"Mr. Low! I did not know you were here. Wouldn't it have been possible to have spared him this ?" '

"I had no option," he said. "I was away on the Continent when it happened, and only heard of the regrettable affair yesterday when I hurried back. I made inquiries, but found that he must be buried here according to regulations." He spoke lies, but how was she to know. She said nothing more about it, but he walked by her side down to the gates, and insisted upon taking her back to the town with him in the cab he had brought. There they parted, but not before he had obtained her address in London and made her promise to let him know when she had found an engagement to her liking.

div.head: CHAPTER XXXIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXIII.
MAKING 017 TUB BONDS..

The nest few weeks were busy ones with Douglas Low. So long as he was but steward in his cousin's interests so long might the estates take their own chance and go to the wall. But now that he had come into the property he - set about putting affairs to rights and endeavouring to retrieve the failing fortunes of Fenwick Chase.

Lawyer Pryke 'was not slow to clutch with a greedy claw as much of the pickings as, by artful. stretching of the law, he could claim. Frequent were the bickerings between the. old money-grubber and the new heir. One day, however, the haggling developed into an open quarrel, and in an unguarded moment Low raised his fist and dealt the old man a blow.

Lawyer Pryke's face turned livid with evil fury and hate. He shook his skinny fit in Low's face. "You whelp, you, to strike an old man like me You think I am helpless, but you don't know. I have been your best friend. When suspicions have been afoot who has quieted them? Jabes Pryke. You forget that I hold the secret to much of your doings. Who ruined old Hendon? I know the details. And I know why. And there are more

tinge I want to know, more serious tinge. BUIL You have struck me, who never sufferqd an ilk dignity to go unavenged, and I'll move Heaven anel earth but what I'll have ray revenge on you, Douglas Low, for that act." The old man's face was distorted with evil passion as he said these words. He foamed at the mouth and he shook like an aspen, not with fear but with the revengeful malice within him. He was a dangerous foe, and Low regretted the act, and would have apologised, but old Pryke, seizing his stick, stumped off out of the house and would listen to nothing. Henceforth he was a dangerous enemy. Yet Low knew he was not likely to say anything about the Hendon affair, for his own name would not go scatheless. And what else did he know or was likely to know? Pshaw I It was foolish to give the old man a second thought. But Pryke nursed the rankling enmity. He had often asked himself strange questions about two events—the fire at Hendon's granaries, and, to go still furl ter back, the mysterious tragedy which had lost his old client, Mr. Fenwick, his life. He had never liked Martin Fenwick ; he was too sharp and there was nothing to be made out of him. But now that the young fellow was dead, he experienced a pang of regret that he had not done his duty by the estates which he, as legal adviser, ought to have safeguarded, instead of joining in with Low to rob them.

lie had been among the last to believe Martin Fenwick guilty, and as the family solicitor had taken up the case with considerable spirit. But the force of evidence was against them, and even his belief in the young man's innocence had given way before the trial was over. The vindictive character of the old gipsy's evi- dence was what puzzled him most, but he had never dreamt that it was perjured evidence. What struck him as even more odd, was the sudden friendship that sprung up between Low, who it would only have been natural to suppose would have held his cousin's accusers in everlasting enmity, and the gipsies, mother and son. But even that circumstance had long passed from his mind in the absorbing business of robbing the V'enwick estate. Now, however, smarting under the insult he had received, his"old problems concerning Low and the gipsies, and Martin Fenwick came to mind. If by any means he could do Low an injury, and escape himself, he meant to do it. He had had ample revenge on others who had merely crossed his path. This young man should find that he could not insult and strike him with impunity. He had been in this "frame of mind about a week when he received a letter from an unknown correspondent in the South of France.

"Dear sir,—l am compiling a book upon crime mysteries, and I have been told that you were engaged in what has long been regarded as s strange case, that of the murder of Mr. Fenwick, of Fenwick Chase. Would it be giving you too much trouble to instruct your clerk to buy copies of back numbers of all the papers giving full reports of the tragedy and the trial, and to forward the same with a short resume giving your opinion and views of the various points in the evidence. I enclose a cheque for five guineas, which shall be further supplemented if it does not meet your cllarges. —I am, yours faithfully, ROBERT WEBSTER."

"` Robert Webster.' Never heard the name before that I know of. Humph! Interesting book I should fancy. Yes, I'll tell Jobson to get all the papers he can this morning, and send them off at once. Five guineas. Humph I Quarter of an hour's dictation. Not bad pay. I wonder if he would spring another five. I'll pad it out a bit and try him, though I don't suppose there is anything fresh to say. I'd like to read that book." Lawyer Pryke did not visit Fenwick again, but there were many items of business which Low was, perforce, obliged to write about. Little by little the affairs of the estate were cleared up, and Low found himself getting daily more secure, and although much of the Most available property had been turned into ready cash, still there was quite sufficient to enable him to live at ease and-.-he turned the thought over with con- siderable pleasure—to marry Grace. "She is sure to accept now that Martin is dead," he said to himself. "if only—But there can be, shall be, no ifs 'in the matter. Kitty Lane—let her rave, let her threaten as much as she likes. A mere tool, a plaything. She answered my pur- pose, and might have proved more useful still if she had stayed on at the post-office instead of worrying her head about, weddings. Ha! ha! ha! A pretty little joke. Hallo who's that? Why can't they let me alone? Hello, it! There's been somebody at that infernal bell the whole day long. Well, who is it ?" "Mr. Parr, sir."

"Tell Mr.' Parr to go to—and—better shew him up, though. I'll settle accounts with Mr. Zeke Parr once and for all," he added to himself as the man left the room. "I'll be hanged if I'll live in this purgatory with that hang-dog scoundrel always holding threats over my head, any longer. Come in. Well, what the goodness is it this time? " "I haven't visited yer for a long time now, Mr. Low. But I guess yer know the object of my little afternoon call. The usual, rhino. It do run out quickly, don't it, Mr. Low? It wants a week till the next advance, I know, but jest a tanner to keep the pot boiling till then." Low stood up. His guest had settled down into the most comfortable easy-chair as was his wont. "Look here, Parr," said Low, "I'm downright dead sick of you, and everything and everybody that appertains to you." "All right. All right," said Mr. Parr, affably. “Them words ain't very comfortin'. is there any more of it?"

"There is more of it. I've stood this blaCk- loading for years, and I've determined, to cut the story short, to stand it no longer." Parr looked up sharply. "Wota that? "he asked, insolently. "Wots that? "

. "You heard," said Low. "That's my decision. You will get just one ten-pound note more out of me, so that you shan't be stranded without notice. For the t future you will have to work for your living, or go to the deuce for it. This bank stops payment." "Oh, that's the cut of it, is it ? " said Ezekiel Parr. "I suppose yer prepared to stand the consequences?" "Consequences be hanged There are none." "We'll see about that," said Parr. "Don't you offer any threats. If you do, by James, I'll have you in gaol inside twenty-four hours of your uttering them! I'm starting to Play a new hand from to-day. I'm going straight, and I'm not to be blackmailed by any old fake you think you can rake up against me. Last week I was made a magistrate. The word of a Justice of the Peace will be regarded as worth twenty tales told by a crew like you. So go ahead and do your worst. But I warn you of consequences. Con- sider the tables turned."

Parr stared in blank amazement at this unex- pected speech. "Well, I'm blowed I" he gasped, And lapsed into silent astonishment again. "There," said Low, "there's a ten-pound note. It's the last hush-money you'll ever get from me. You'd better turn your attention to some honest method of livelihood. Please also to cease familiarities with me. Don't call. I shall always be out if you do. Don't speak to me in the street. The cottage is yours; do what you like with it. But for the future we are strangers. It's getting late. Good-night." He pointed to the door, but Parr still remained staring blankly at the note in his hand. "Say, 'ere," he said presently, as Low aroused him with a gesture of impatience, "you're only jokin', gov. You'll be all Sir Garnet in a day or two. Sorne'ut upset yer, I'll bet. Well, 'ere's off. Good-night."

div.head: WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB The Prospects for Next Season. --- Annual Meeting.
div.p: WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB The Prospects for Next Season. --- Annual Meeting.
Mr J L Williams presided Gver the annual cooptiLg of the Warrington AS3ociatior. Foothll Club which was held at the Patten Arms Hotel on Motriay iv. uit,g,. Thys_was a moderate attet.dance. _

Mr NORMAN, asaidant tro;4surer, said that they had hoped to hive had the pr.'se.nce of Mr Sharplfs, of Charley, president of the Lancashire le ague at that ineeting,, but for same reason which he , (Mr Normal.) was unable to .-xplain that gentleman had not arrived. Continuing he said that•they bad a meeting a few days ago to discuss the finances of the ,chlib,and it was decided that what- ever deficit ttere was—and there was a considerable deficit—sboald be accounted for by the old Committee, so that the new Committee to be elected could commeuce their duties with an entirely free hand, and need not trouble themselves as to financial obligations.

THE PROSPECTS OF THE CLUB. ELECTION OF A NEW PRESIDENT. The Cumin Law said that on the whele, he thought the supporters of the Association game in Warrington could congratulate themselves. The past season had been a very arduous one from many standpoints, but he thought, that considering the circumstances the club had come through very well. This was mainly due to the efforts of the committee, Messrs Elliott, Bradshaw. and Norman in particular. Then again they had hao .Lt the President a geuLAlngn who loan shown himself to be an out and out sportsman. (Hear, hear.) If any- thing had been wanting Councillor Pierpoint had been willing to place not, only his services at the disposal ; of the committee, but in his son they had had one who bad helped considerably to give a fillip to the game in Warrington. In winning the Warrington Cup the club had accomplished a very good stroke of business. This was the second time in the history of the Warring- ton and District Football Association that a Warrington Club had won the cup. He thought that now there was nothing wanting but for the new committee to t,:ke up their daties in no half hearted manner,but to go on work- ing with the greatest energy, so that at the next annual meeting they should not be in such a financial position as they were on the present occasion. There seemed to be a growing impresreon in Wasrington that they were trying to injure the Rugby game, but speaking person- ally, he thought that was the farthest object from their minds. They only wished to encourage the Association game, and they were willing on all occasions to meet the Rugby Club and arrange that when their first team was playing at home the Association team should play away. By so doing the fixtures would not clash. Enthusiasts would then have the opportunity of seeing first-class football in the respective codes each Saturday. In join- ing the Lancashire League he thought the committee had taken a step in the right direction. All that was wanting was the finance to carry it through. That meeting owed a debt of gratitude to the officers fa 'he admirable manner in which they had conducted tne affairs of the club during the past season. Councillor Pierpoint did not see his way to again occupy the position of President, so he (the chairman) proposed the name of one whom he thnught would take a very active interest in the club—Colonel W Hall Walker, M.P., (Applause.) Mr G ELLIOTT seconded the propesition, which Was unanimously agreed to.
_ THE VICE-PRESIDENT. On the suerrestion o! the CHAIRMAN. the election of the Vice-Presidents was left in the ,hands of the Corsmittee.

div.head: ELECTION OF COMMITTEE..
div.p: ELECTION OF COMMITTEE..

_ The election of the committee was amp proceeded witb,but much difficulty was experienced In inducing a sufficient number of gentlemen to accept the office. Mr KIERNAN mentioned that in joining the Lancashire League the club would lessen their travelling expenses as the places which they would visit would not be so far distant as the towns included in the Combination fixtures. He also mentioned that last year the first match of the season was a tremendous success and if they had gone CD like that during the season they should have had a handsome balance in hand, probably a couple of hundred pounds, and would have been able to go into the open market and buy their men. After considerable discussion the following committee was elected :—Messrn J L Wißiams.Elliott seri., Bennett Pritchard, Martin, Elliott jun., Kiernan. Woodcock,. Dicks, Cex, Bradshaw (secretary), Payton, Forbes and Cuter. This concluded the businees.

div.head: COUNCILLOR AND HIS -COUNSEL
div.p: COUNCILLOR AND HIS -COUNSEL

-- COUNCILLOR JOHN CHESTERFIELD was elected a mem-1 bee of the corporation of Rotherham, Yorkshire, in Jubilee year of 1887. P.•pular, a thoroughly good busi- ness man, he is noted in the eounail chamber for quiet consistent work. div.head: CHAPTER XX-W.
div.p: CHAPTER XX-W.
EUREKA!

Three months had passed since the escape -trui death of the unfortunate convict at Smilehunt and the matter had long since ceased to be a shbject for discussion in the village. The new squire had been remarkably diligent about the estate—a marked contrast to his attitude when he was but holding the property in trust. He had become more and more buoyant as the days passed away, and he found that the woman Parr was inclined to let the matter of the murder drop. He had only seen the old gipsy once, and she had curtseyed to him with marked deference. But he had not looked behind him after be had passed, or he would have seen si,skinny fist shaking in the air at him, and the old haa's bloodless lips moving in curses upon him. He congratulated himself upon the effect of the bold front he had assumed. He had dismayed the Parrs, and shaken off old Pryke. His freedom was just commencing. There was but one thing lacking to consummate his happiness—he wanted Grace. More than ever did his old passion burn within him. There could be no lasting satisfaction until she was mistress of Fenwick Chase. •
He had waited to give her time to recover from the blow of Martin's death. Three months were surely enough, he argued to himself. Ha would

He had some difficulty 10 finding GrAce, but at length he traced her t 0,3 cheap lodging-house in Peckham. She was mother help to the landlady, and assisted in the manage' ment of five unruly children and ia waiting LIP° a houseful of boarders. When Low set eyes upon her he staggered at her appearance. She was more pallid th; her cheeks were sunken, and a sad expres: told of internal suffering, of heartache, o lessness, revealed itself only too clearly u, features.

div.head: CHAPTER XXXV.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXV.

THE EXTRAORDINARY HAPPENINGS AT THE Douglas Low rose with a light heart on Mond ,_l4 morning. The weather was crisp and health imparting, and he made a hearty breakfast. !, had not seen Grace yet, for he had been away wile: she arrived, and had only returned late on Sundo,,, night. But there had been a note awaiting him the Chase from her, and he knew that she wool' not fail to meet him at the church. The wedding was to take place at eleven, and he had an hour to spare, for he had breakfasted earlt The morning was so, inviting that he took a turn m* the grounds. He walked on through the slirtibS- and over th lawns until he reached a wicket gate that led cloy; to the hollow beyond. It was in that hollow had met Kitty Lane. The memory of it Caine bed to him now, and he leant over the gate lost reflection upon the turn of events. He had - . _ _ _

"Mornin', squire. Tell your fortune to-deli It's hard times that have fallen upon old Jezebel with her son in the lock-up again, and nothio comin' in. Just cross her palm, and give her help of a shillin'—just this once, being as it's squire's wedding day." Low's brow contracted, for before him, witb 6 mocking smile upon her face, was the old beg' Jezebef Parr. "Go away, woman. Don't come to me with,. your fooling. Here, go and drink the bride health on that." He pitched her half-a-crown, and turned on heel. But she seized the coin, and, in a mottle° of wild rage, threw it after him, shrieking nirialg curses into his ear as he went. It was an e omen, meeting that wretched woman, he thotigb;_'e He wished he had not gone out. What did mean by such a sudden outburst of spleen? Sur' not to-day, of all days, would she-- But wbe if she did? He could brave her out. To his surprise and di•gust, it crowded, and a string of villagers hung about,.# doorway. div.head: ADULTERATED GIN.
div.p: ADULTERATED GIN.
Publican Fined at Warrington. _— Mr. Browne and Teetotal Magistrates.

Elizabeth Monks, the licencee of the Packet House Inn, Bridge-street, was summoned at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, for selling to the prejudice of Ralph Norman a pint of gin. which was adulterated with water to the extent of 43 per cent, and was there- fore not ot the nature, substance and quality demanded by the purchaser.—The Deputy-Town clerk (Mr Stanley Wilson) conducted the prosecution, and the defendant was represented by Mr A Browne. At the outset Mr Wilson briefly related the feats of the case and produced a certificate of analysis given by Dr Guest Garnet, to the effect that the gin was adulterated with water, boing 43 degreesl under proof, or eight degrees more than was allowed by Act of Parliament. Evidence was thetecalled, the first witness being Giles Buckley, who informed the court that, acting on the in- structions of Inspector Norman he visited the Packet House Inn, on the 23rd May at about four o'clock and asked for a pint cf gin.for which he paid 2. Witness walked to the door, and was met by Mr Norman who went back with him into the house and spoke to the defendant about the transaction.—By Mr Browne: He handed the gin to Inspector Norman. He could read a little, but he ,did not notice the card (now produced which bore the following notice :—" Food and Drugs Adulteration,Ant .38 and 39 Vic, Notice. All spirits sold in this establishment are of a superior quality, but diluted according to price. No alcoholic strength guaranteed. By order." He was not pre- pared to dispute that the netice was exhibited. Inspector Norman said he instructed the last witness to purchase the gin. Witness went into the house after the purchase, and the defendant admitted to him that she had sold the liquor to Buckley and that she had been paid 2s for it. He told her that it was his intention to submit it tollle public analyst and left the defendant a third of the gin. He submitted the other portion of the gin to Dr Guest Cornell, and the result was the analysis which had been read. He did not see the notice produced by Mr. Browne. For the defence, Mr. Browne said some of his clients had been summoned for exceedingly trivial cases, but this was one of the Most trivial which had ever been brought into court. His client had been summoned for having added 8 per cent, of water to the gin. He would show the Bench what that meant, and Mr Browne did so by holding up two bottles, one of which contained gin and the other a small quantity of water. A similar demonstration, he explained, was made at the Dares- bury Petty Sessions, and the Bench came to the conclu- sion to dismiss the case, and he asked the presnnt Bnnch to act Its a similar manner. Could such a ridiculous quentity of water be to the prejudice of any purchaser ? The thing was absurd. Apart from that, the notice which he had produced was exhibited in the public. house. After quoting a case in support of his contention Mr Browne stated that the notice was prepared purposely to cover that particular case. It was a notice that was put in the most conspicuous place in the public-house, and no one could enter without seeing it. It would be idle for anyone to say they did not see it. Moreover defendant was summoned for selling to the prejudice of Ralph Norman,whereas the purchaser was Giles Buckley and not *Norma. The defendant was a respectable licensed ' .victualler and had kept the house for 16 years. Samples of liquor had been taken from time to time,and not a single complaint had been made until now against her. The sale of the gin was a pure mistake. She bought ltlf gallons of gin two years ago, and lately took a gallon out:of the cask to put in the bar. preperly reducing the liquor as she thought. Subsequently it transpired that the liquor had gone down ot its own accord. It was well known that all spirits would go down even while in bond in a few months' time. He hoped, therefore, that in these circumstances the Bench would dismiss the case. He was spe iking to two teetotalers on the Bench, and-- Mr Thornton: I don't think you should make such a remark. It should be withdrawn. The Chairman : We are not temperance people here, . . .
Mr Thornton :
The remsrk should be withdrawn.

Mr Browne: But it is well known you cannot dis- tinguish-- Alderman Heaton : She is summoned for putting more water in the gin than she ought to have done. There is as much fraud as in putting in threc times as much water. Mr Thornton : The quantit3 of water may sePin little. We are here te do justice, and the remark of Mr Browne ought to he withdrawn. Mr Browne: I have said nothing wrong. Mr Thornton : You had ;no right to make such a statement. ' The Chairman: I don't think you ire correct in your comments. Alderman Heaton: lam not a teetotaler nor do I intend to be. Mr Browne: It is an absurd quantity of water to put into the gin. If you were to drink the gin yourself you could not distinguish it. Alderman Heaton: That is not the question. A fine of lOs and costs was inflicted—in all 21 ss.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

GALLANT RESCUE FROM DROWNING.—A plucky rescue from drowning was effected at Stockton Heath, at seven o'clock on Friday evening. It appears tliat a little boy, named Charles 'inches, the four year old sou of Charles Hughes painter, 12, Old London-road, was playing on the bank of the Bridgewater Canal near the lock when 46 slipped and fell into the water. Fortu- nately he was seen struggling by John Lowe, the lock keeper, who, without divesting hinhelf of any clothing plunged into the water, which at this point height feet in depth. He got hold of the child and succeeded in handing it to some men who were standing on the bank. Neither the child nor the rescuer were any the worse for their immersion. It is stated that this is the sixth or seventh rescue from drowning which Lowe has ' effected, the last one being at Latchfoid twelve months ago.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT PEN KETH. Speech by Mr. H. Cameron, M.P.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT PEN KETH. Speech by Mr. H. Cameron, M.P.
The Work of the Government.

" Where the present Government has brouzhc Us" WAR the subject of an address delivPre4 h M R Cameron, M P, in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Penkoth, on Monday evening. There was a large attendance. At the outset, Mr Dodds said it was now 30 years since he had the honour of making the acquainraire of Mr Cameron. In the North of England Mr Cameron's name was a household word. ELI was a leader in every movement that made for the good of the people, for the amelioration of the condition of the poor,for their educa- tion, and every good ob'ect in regard to public and social matters. He (Mr Dodds) bad frequently had him as a guest, and as he was staying with him at Penketh for a few days, he thought they would be pleased to hear him speak on public questions. Whatever view Mr , Cameron might take, it would be the view of an honest man, and whatover opinions he gave expression to, whether they agreed with them or not, they might be satisfied that Mr Cameron held them in his heart and conscience. (Hear, hear). Mr R Garnett then took the chair and briefly introduced the speaker. MR. CAMERON'S SPEECH. Mr. Cameron, M.P. who bad a cordial reception, said that, whether to his advantage or disadvantage, he took a very decided stand on the great question ot the time. He;laad fought an election upon it, and he said, without any boasting, that while the important constituency he represented shared the war enthusiasm, his maj irity at the election was increased from 800 to 1,900 odd. (Hear, hear.) e had fought for a principle which to him was a very important one. He wished to speak with the utinost ,lrankness and candour. The present Govern- ment came into power in 11115 with a great majority, and on promises many of which, he thought they did not intend to fulfil. There was no idea of war then, but since they ha 4 been in office they had had two great ,1 wars and four small ones, so that it looked like a war- like Government. There was nothing wonderful in that, because it had always been that the difference between Toryiam and Liberalism was that while under Liberal- ism th emphasis was mainly laid upen the condition of the people at home, the characteristic of Toryistn was a spirited foreign policy. England was' essentially an industrious country, and peace was the great and chief element under which we could grow and prosper, and that was a general principle which any tioyernment ought to consider. LORD SALISIIIURY'S GRACEPTIL CINCESSIONS.”

The present Government commenced to show none of that spirit but he regretted to say that their first deal- ings with foreign powers did us no good. We bad treaties with two or three places where we had impore teat trade but Lord Salisbury thought it wisdom to give many graceful concessions to those people with I whom we have commercial treaties. M ‘daeasoar was one. We had a great trade with that island even after the Franck rionquest, awl we had an arrangement that our goods should be admitted at a certain tariff. That tariff was raised by the French and practically excluded our trade. Unfortunately Lord Salisbu.v yielded weakly and a large trade, especially from Llyerpool I became worthless by his weakness. Lord Salisbdry did exactly the same thing in regard to Tunis and Siam and his action had been detrimental to our trade. soon afterwards the war between Greece and Turkey broke out and many of them thought that if England sym- pathised anywhere she ought to sympathise with the oppressed. England's voice ought to have sunken out then. If one grand old man, whose memory they ven- erated, bad been living, that voice would have been heard. (Hear, hear.) The only satisfactory feature in connection with that war was the Settlement in regard 1 to Crete. TRH DOLES TO LANDLORDS AND CLERGY

The home policy of the Goverment was such as he considered could not receive the approval of thoughtful Conservatives. He was sure Hit waS put to them 'definitely to say whether the Government of this 'country should legislate for or give special benefits or doles to any class of the community unless that class was in urgent need through distress of some form or 1 another they would answer hi the negative, Yet we had seen aid given to landlords who did not need it, The relief given to the landlords inflicted a serious I burden upon the ratepayers of the great towns, who were, through their town councils,protessing vigorously against the renewal of the Act. It cost London £262,000 a year, Manchester £33,000, Sheffield £21,000, Bradford £14,000, and other towns in prooorition, and it meant that in some cases id. and in other cases 21. in the pound was added to the rates. It was stated that this relief was intended for the farmer, but Mr Chaplin had said himself th st there was no doubt the money would ultimately find its way into the pockets of the landlord. When the shipbuilding trade was distressed the G )vern- ment never thought of giving them a dole He ventured to say that the relief had born given by the wrong parties and given on unjust and unsound principles. Aid was also given to the clergy and immunity to the publi- cans, and the reason for all this class legislation was in- dicated by Lord George Hamilton when be said the Government were going to " safeguard the interests of their friends." The clergy were their friends. Be had nothitv, to say against the clergyman. Religion was trite and beneficial and those who received the benefit of it should put their hands into their pockets and pay ' the man who minietered to them in spiritual things. There was no need for State aid to State•plid clergy. ' Because the farmers were hard up and unable to pay the tithes was that any reason why the State should be called upon to relieve the clergymen by taking off half the rates to the tune of £lOl,OOO ? IPDII7IIITY TO "THE TRADE." Included in the friends of the Governm-mt were the brewers and publicans. The liquor trade took great interest in politics. They busied themselves and made most of their big publie-housies committee rooms. Beer went and who paid for it one did not know. It was a mystery. (Laughter.) The beer seemed to flow almost through the streets and the publicans, with very few exceptions, voted against the Liberal candidates. They voted against him (Mr Camsron). They knew he was a teetotaler and therefore a dangerous person to their trade. For the last six years the Government had stood upon the licensed victualling trade and he did not think that was a sound foundation for any Government. (Hear, hear.) The Government cared noshing for the evils wrought by the drink trade, as was shown by their inaction in regard to the reports of the Licensing Commission and what was known as the Children's Bill, which was demanded by all classes of the com- munity and carried by a majority of 315 on the second reading. He hoped something would come out of Ciese efforts for temperance, and he would take any measure that would help to mitigate the terrible evils of drink ; but, why, he asked, should the country struggle for it In this fashion ? They were loath to offend their friends and the immunity to the publicans was how they had rewarded them.
RETEOGRLDE EDUC&TIONAL POLICY.

Then in the matter of education the of the Government had been of a retrograde character. They knew the need of education. Unlesi oar young men took heed and saw to it that they were equal to their competitors in skill and technical knowledge, and
them

lunless they he ,c abreast with the SWIS9, the German an I the French in education. they would know where E 'gland would be in ano,.her generation. (Hear, hear). Toe education of the country was most imperfect. We had had two educational bills since 1895. The first was so imperfect* RI biassed, and is intention 110 obvious, that the beat friends of che Government cried "shame" upon it, and it was dropped in a hurry. The chief feattue of the now bill showed what the Government was. They had never loved the school boards, Mr Bal- four had said. he b-

Salisbury bad stated that it was the duty of .the present Government, in their new education proposals, to " capture the school boards." What was the fault of the school boar ts ? It was their marvellous success. There had never been in the history of this country an education given to the working classes to compare with that which had been given to them in the last twenty years in the great towns of England. (Hear, hear). He admitted that in small districts where the rateable value was low that school boards had not been .as efficient as in the large towns. In the large centres, the school ooard had been the most marvellous educational power in this country. Some of the Board School boys had gone to the colleges and taken degrees. Others had risen to be Mayors, lawyers, preachers, doctors and even members of Parliament. How did they sewage to do it without a catechism ? How did they manage to do it without a formal creed? fin ven- tured to say from his knowledge as Chairman of one of the largest school boards in his district that the board sehools had produced as pious men and as pious women as ever came out of a church school By the new education bill, the Government wanted, in the words of Dr Macnamara to truncate the School Board system. The result of Cockerton decision was chat the Scoool B oard had no right to pay jot anything but the elementary branches of education, and if they did more they were breaking the law. It was Lord Cecil who discovered this wonderful illegality on the part of the School Boards. The continuation classes had been conducted by School Boards as supplementary work for the past t weave years, and to stop it now would lead to great confusion. The Government had brought in a new bill making provision for these continuation classes to exist on condition that the second part of the bill estabr fishing County Councils as the educational authority fo the secondary schools, was passed. That was a bribe ; a contemptible bribe. There was not a true educationa: list in the House of Commons who would take it on that condition. They must have national education on a real footing. Let religion be taught but without viola- tion of conscience. He was one of those who believed that a parable of Christ was worth all the catechisms that man ever composed He believed a Psalm of David committed to memory was better than all the formulas. A pplause.) THE 11AR IN SOUTH AFRICA Coming to the question of the war, the speaker said he supposed there would be jingoes present. If there were any, perhaps they objected to the word jingo. He hoped they did as he objected to the word, pro-Boar. He was not pro•Boer' be was pro-justice, and he hoped they understood the distinction: He was pro-justice to his enemies, and pro-justice that the truth might be found out, so that all this terrible business: might be stopped: The origin of the war was being found out every day. Re objected to the war for the reason that he believed if there had been no Rhodes and no great com- panies speculating in gold and seeking great dividends, and no Jameson Reid, there would have been no war. (Applause.) That was as self-evident to him as the sun shining on a Midsummer day. Referring to the nego- tiations between the Boers and the Colonial Office prior to the war, Mr Cameron pointed ont that nine-tenths of concessions asked for by Mr. Chan* irlain were granted. It had been said that the Dutch in S ,uth Africa wanted to clear the English out of the country, bit if that was true why did not the Boers do so when they had the chance after defeating the British army? The simple truth was, the Beers saw by the Jameson raid that the independence of their country was threatened and they immediately commenced to arm themselves. There was not a particle of evidence that the Boers imported ammu- nition and arms before the Jameson raid. It was after that that the Boers armed themselves to the teeth. The British Govornmnnt received information that the Boers were arming, and the question would PerbaPsbe asked. "why didn't we take steps to counteract it." They had the reply from Mr Balfour, who stated that," our mouths were closed by the raid." That being so it was the duty of the government to prepare for eventualities. Instead of that our brave soldiers who were sent out to South Africa were unjustly treated by being driven to a x war totally unprepared, for their guns were ontranged by the enemy and there was insufficient hospital accommodation, resulting in the death of twice as many soldiers from fever as from the , bullets of the enemy. By this war we bad set two races in South Africa in deadly antagonism. We were Paying an awful price in blood and treasure. The devastation and misery inflicted upon the country Were incalculable and the Boers had come to the terrib'e alternative rather to die than to yield. Let them look at the country.with its burned farms, the families of the Boers herded to gether in concentration camps, with a percentage of deaths amongst tbe women and children horrible to think of. Lt them use a little imagination and try to see with their own eyes what it was that had been ac- complished by the present Government. He feared if Lord &Hiner was to go back to South Africa there would he no peace. The Boers would never give in so long as he was there: They had got into their heads an intense antipathy to him. He was a gond, a wise, and an able man in many respec's, but he did not act on his own Initiative. He was moved by a power behind, and if they inquired at Birmingham they would ascertain where the headquarters of that power were. (Applause) It was a terrible problem they had now to face. What was to be the future of the country ? By present methods South Africa would become another Ireland. The Government policy had not only been wicked but bungling, which was almost worse. Men of sympathy and with feelings of humanity were wanted to re—build the country, and to secure its well-being in the future. With a Liberal Government many problems would be solved which the present Government would never solve either at home or abroad. By wise administration at home this England would prosper and grow, and just as Eoglishmen were treated and developed to manhood at home so would they be enabled to exert a like influence over the whole world. (Applause./ Mr Dodds proposed a vote of thanks to Mr Cameron and referred to the able and eloquent address he bad given them. The Rev John Gunnell seconded the vote of thanks and said it did not follow that they agreed with every sentiment which had been expressed. He hardly thought the lecturer would expect that. Mr C 'moron had given them a number of loud-speaking facts and they would go away from the meeting better instructed on the political condition of things in the country. The Chairman paid be endorsed the remarks made. He estimated Mr Cameron very highly. The vote was unanimously carried. Mr Cameron acknowledged the eompliment, and proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was heartily carried. The meeting then terminated. -4TCLIIB I IMMENSE BARGAINS. div.head: GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.
A Booking Office Wanted.

A meeting of the Grea', S inkey Parish Council was held on Tuesday evening in the Board Schools, Mr George Thompson (chairman) presiding, and there were also present Messrs T Halton, Fulton Smith, Bilshaw, Taylor, Singleton, and J Smith (clerk.)
NIJMBERING OF H .1:79E9.
The Clerk stated that th—e Is-ouses had been numbered as instructed by the Council at the former meeting. Most of them now bad tablets on. LETTER FROM TME POSTMASTER OF WARRINGTON

The Clerk read the following letter from Mr yiney, Postmaster of Warrington :--" June sth. Dear Sir,— Please convey to your Council; my thanks and apprecia tion for the vote of thanks-which-they have been good enough to accord me." Mr Smith said that the letter, which was addressed to him, was in reply to one from the Council thanking Mr Vines, for his attention to the requests of the Council for increased postal facilities for the district. THE BOOKING ARRANGEMENTS AT THE STATIrEC

- MR. MELDRUM'S LETTER NOT SATISFACTORY. 'The Clerk said he wrote to Mr Meldrum,of Liverpool, on behalf of the Council, asking for some immediate modification of the present booking arrangements at Sankey Station. Mr Meldrum had replied as follows : —'in further reply.to the letter of the 3rd inst relative to the request made by your Council for some modifi- cation in the present booking office arrangements at Sankey Station, I have been endeavouring as far as possible to asaertain what it is your Council wish, because you do not enter into any details in giving ex- pression to your grievance, and hence it has only been by incoiring of the stationmaster that I have ascer- tained to some extent what It is you complain about. I am told that it is bscause the booking office is fixed on the down side of the station, but if we were to transfer it t o the up skis it would be equally hard for passengers going in the direction of Widnes and Liver- pool as it is for passengers at the prest.gt time to cross to the down side to book for the direction of Warring- ton. and if we were to comply with the request made by your Board we should simply have complaints from another section of the puhlio. If this is really the point which vour Board wish to bring under my notice lam afraid I shall not be able to do anything to assist them." The Chairman : It is rather a strange letter in 'my opinion: I hardly think that the stationmaster at Great Sankey would give any opinion to Mr Sdeldrum to lead him to suppose the Council thought of eemoiing the present booking office. On the other hand we wing a booking office on the other side. Mr Falton Snait : I d tnink it is al answer at all.

The Chairman: It is a most serious matter, and the oftener Igo to the station the more I see the danger that evists. However, if anything now hap pens we shall feel that we are not to blame. Mr Fulton Smith: We are not railway experts and I don't see that the company should expect us to tell them what they should do. Wa have punted out the danger that exists, and a different letter might have been sent by the representative of a big coinoany like the Cheshire Lines Committee.

The Clerk : I dif rist ) into detsils,heoause I thought my letter explained it.olf. Mr. Hatt •in thouzhc a fusther let,er should be sent asking Mr Meldrnm how long tnn boskin offi le should los kept open bsfore a train was due, to enable passen- gers to gPt tickets Ssin-tirnes a train was in the station only half a minute.
Mr Singleton : Ind there was a wish to avoid an accident bap,,ening while passengers were crossing the 1 me.

_ _ Mr Fulton Smith: The object of our latter was to draw attention to tha dancer which exists, so that the committee front their poaltion c )uld make exhaustive Inquiries and ascertain wnether pAssengers had time after getting their tickets to get to the train. mOn the motion of Mr Halton, seconded by Mr Single- ton, it was decided that a further letter be written to Mr Meldrurn, miring how long the ticket office was kept open before the departure of a train.

MORE AlO3-17T SANKEY nnonx. Mr Singleton said the smell from Sankey Brook during the past seven days had been disgraceful. The Clerk read some corrnaxind .nce which had taken place on the subject. He had w :Men to the Town Clerk of Warrington telling him that written and verbal complaints had been received b 7 tie Council about the condition of the brook, and he asked him to take steps to remedy the nuisance. Ele had also written to the Clerk to the Rural District Council suggesting that the Council and the Corporation should take up the matter jointly. A further letter had been forwarded to the Clerk to the Lancashire County Council asking him to take the matter up. Kr Sutton had replied that the &Mica! Officer, Surveyor and Inspeutor of the Warring- ton Rural District hid been authorised to visit St. Helens and reprt-upon the nuisance, whileldr Whittle had intimated that the matter had been placed In the hands of the Depute Medical Officer. Mr I T Muspratt deputy-clerk of the Lancashire County Council, had promised that the matter should be brought before the Health Committee. Mr Halton said he was afraid that the Council were powerless in the matter, The contributors to the nuisance were the Warrington Town Council and the Rural District Council. What, therefore, could they expect in these circumstances? The brook was tapped at so many hundred yards, and Mr Sutton said the Cor- poration were guilty' of turning sewage into the brook and also the Warrington Rural District Council. The Chairman thought the Sankey Council were in- debted to Mr Halton for the manner in which he intro- duced the subject at the meeting of the District Council at Warrington. Be (the speaker) was at a loss to understand how any public body could be qulea with regard to such a nuisance. The Town Council load taken over Little Sankey with great profit to themselves and had now to deal with the brook, and they should take their fair share in trying to cleanse it. Mr Halton : The Corporation are part owners of the brook. The Clerk: The Warrington and Sankey Brcok. (& laugh). The Chairman : / don't think there is any other place in the United Kingdom where such a stream would be allowed to run through such a thickly popu- lated district as ours without Some action being taken to abate the nuisance. If nothing else can be done the property owners ought to appeal to the Local Govern- ment Board. Mr Singleton : Who in to blame in the matter: Mr Halton: The brook is tapped by rural and urban authorities the whole of the way. The Chairman observed that the question would not be allowed to drop. He would summora another meet- ing when the Clerk had received ftirther replies from the authorities mentioned. A °RUT IMPROVEMENT. Mr Singleton commented upon the great improvement at Penketh-lane end owing to the widening. of the road. The Chairman : Yes, it is the greatest Improvement in the district.
Ur Singleton : If any work in the world required carrying out it was at that particular spot. This was all the public business.

div.head: AT PADGATE
div.p: AT PADGATE

Unfortunately the enjoyment of the children who participated in the annual school treat at Padgate was greatly marred by the wretched atmOspherio conditions which were experienced during the evening. The event which is lo3ked forward to with a feeling of pleasurable anticipation by the juveniles of the village, took place on Saturday. As usual the most complete preparations had beeo made, and many of the inhabitants had adorned their premises with bright flags and bunt- ing. The scholars assembled at their respective schools and the little preliminaries having been completed the procession moved off promptly at two o'clock. This year it had been agreed that the Wesleyan' should have the place of honour so they took the lead headed by the Buckley-street P.S.A. Band. A beautiful silk banner which was purchased only last year, followed, and behind it walked the following ministers and officials:— Revs H G Roberts and T Bishop. and Messrs White, Ward,Jackson and Wright. The cnildren of the industrial School came next, preceded by the band of the school, and the scholars attending Christ Church School brought un the rear: Many o the children carried bannerettes and baskets of flowers and for so small a place the procession was a very creditable one. At the head of the Industrial School portion of the procession walked : Mr A J Jolley (chairman of the Board of Guardians), and Messrs Mather, Wright (master),Jones (assistant master). and Mrs Wright (matron), whilst the Christ Church scholars were preceded by the Revs Pollock—Hill (vicar) and 0 Vale-Owen (Orford), and Messrs Mather (marshal),Grounds, Critchley. Blackwell (schoolmaster); Bennett, and Royston. After parading the village, the children adjourned to the fields where games leo, were indulged in. Unfortu- nately, at about four o'clock a drizzling rain set in, and a general move was made to the schoolrooms, where an excellent tea had been provided, and was thoroughly enjoyed. Rain fell incessantly during the greater part of the evening, thus putting an end to any further out- door enjoYment. Owing to the unfavourable State of the w ether throughout the evening, the sport arranged in connection with the schools were postponed. AM for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGII-CLASS MINBBAL afATHRS.--A,vt

div.head: WALKING DA'
div.p: WALKING DA'
NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Another draw was added to Warrington's record on Saturday but it is some little consolation to know that had the weather permitted the completion of the match, Warrington would probably have secured a victory. The New Brighton contingent came over to the Arpley enclosure, and it was not expected that the home team would have any difficulty in disposing of them. The seaside men were allowed to go to the wicket first, and were all dismissed for the magnificent total of 57. Warrington had barely settled down to their task when the rain des- cended heavily and as it showed no prospect of abat!- stumps were drawn at half past six the home teax. having raised 24 for the loss of two wickets. This was indeed hard lines, for had the match been finished War- rington ought easily to have won. The players waited at the field about two hours in the hope that the down pour would cease but they had to go home disappointed though not defeated. .4.13 t.a.4 •
atmg team I

To come to details the Warrington captain was suc- cessful in naming the right side of the coin, but the visitors were allowed to take first innings. Eskrigge and S F Fitzroy took first turn with the willow, Thewlie and Gibson sharing the bowling. It was soon evident that the visitors did not possess much batting force, several of the batsmen retiring after making very poor exhibitions. Only a single shad been registered when Poch-Yore brought off a fine catch at cover, dismissing Fitzroy. Price filled the vacancy, but his stay was brief, for Thewlis with a fine length ball got rid of the visiting professional, whilst in the same over Davies bad his leg stump disturbed. A J Toone was the next to bat, and several sharp runs were chronicled and double figures had only been hoisted when a smart catch at the wicket was responsi- ble for Eskegge's di-missal. With Huntley as bone's associate a slight stand was made, the batsmen making several short rune and profiting by indifferent returns.
When the aggregate bad reached 28, Dr Smith relieved Gibson in the bowling. Thewlis continued to work havoc with the ball, and.Toone bad to depart after placing 13 to his credit. " freely

Walsh took his place and hit _ and Huntley adopting the same tactics, made four from one of Thowlis'e deliveries. This was his final contribution, for with the next:stroke, he was caught by B Silcock, so that six batsmen were now out for 35.

Walsh continued to show good form and dispatched two successive balls from Thewlis to the boundary. It was left to Dr. Smith to finish off the innings in a sum- mary manner,and after Tranton had been bowled at 44 Walsh took the total to $7. when he was caught at mid- on. G. L. Lloyd and A. W. Healey were dismissed in one over, and the innings closed for 57. Both Thewlis and Dr. Smith acquitted themselves creditably as bowlers, both maintaining a fine length.

J Callon and Thewlis commenced Warrington's innings, against the deliveries of Price and Bind°. The batementin view of the threatening state f the weather showed a tendency to force the game and 20 runs were registered in ten minutes. At 24 Thewlis was taken at short %dip, and J Gibbon arrived to see Callon drive Hind for three when the new corner was bowled. Before Dr Smith could take up his pogition at the crease rain began to fall, and after waiting until half-past six, and there being little hope of the weather taking up, the stumps were drawn.

The Second Eleven bad not even the satisfaction of I senling any of their men in to bat. They journeyed to New Brighton, and the home team winning the toss elected to bat first. The score had reached e 4 for six wickets when rain caused a cessation of play for the day.

Foot Racing. At the Wigan County Police Sports held at Springfield Park on Saturday, Constable Robinson, of the Warring- ton Police Force, ran third, although he started from scratch. E Hilton, of Newton-le-Willows, who is associated with the Sankey Harriers, ran third in the mile race, be being separated by five yards from the second man.
