div.head: Warrington (Cemetery) v. Heatley.
div.p: Warrington (Cemetery) v. Heatley.

That the Warringtonians are going to make a bold bid for championship honours this season was evidenced on Saturday, when at Kersal Moor they administered the soup 4 grace Ito Healey, winning a somewhat hollow victory oy 67 points. From the onset the issue was never in doubt, and Heatley will require a vast deal more experience if they wish to cope successfully with a team of Warrington's reputation. Of the first quartette who occupied the green perhaps the most popular was that recorded by the worthy hon. treasurer to t Warrington team, J r Whittle, whose victory of eleven notches was the result of some fine bowling. From talk ninth end he never allowed Wilson another chance. A rather lengthy game was the outcome of the meeting between T Ellison and W Gould, and it required 30 ends before Ellison was able to cry" game "with a margin of four points in his favour. E Butterworth, jun., gained a meritorious victory over J Bowen, for though behind in the early portion of the game, he stuck to his oppo- nent with dogged pertinacity, and earned the high eulogies expressed for his really substantial victory of six shots. With A J Jones defeating A Dixon by two points, the Heatley cup of sorrow was filled to the brim tor all four games had been lost and they were in minority by 22 points. The experiences of the next quartette were such that Heatley were placed further in arrears, and the substantial victory of J Allison over J Flynn was only a forerunner to more substantial vic- tories. A victory of fifteen points by Allison was equalled by another player in the quartette, T Bolton, whose bowling was marked by a consistent excellence which won the admiration of all. The game between Anderton and J Hollingsworth extended over thirty ends, and the victory of the Warringtonian had more merit in it than the four points show, for his opponent bowled an excellent length. E Taylor made short work lof E Holt, and an eight points victory concluded the second aeries of games, the last lot having results* in an addition of 42 points giving the Warringtonlank the long lead of 64 points. The first reverse experienced by the Warringtonians was incurred by J Ashton, who took an early lead but was passed at the eleventh end and never recovered the lost ground, losing by sin points. Another reverse was sustained when J Harris* succumbed to J Travis by two points, but H Williams more than counterbalanced the reverses when be ac- counted for W Hill by 14 shots, and this too after Williams was five points behind after the first three ends had been trundled. With G Ball defeated_ the Warrinfg tonians lost three out of the last four games played, and ' the number of points in their favour wasi37. Thus nine games out of the twelve were won, and the bowling throughout the afternoon was of a ma, high order. Score Men= 21 L ..... 10

Taints are deep mutter- Liberal Internecine ings of dissatisfaction 10 Troubles. both wings of the Liberal army at the trouble that has broken out in the camp. Of these some are inarticulate and incore sequent,some strenuous and impassioned,and the,' slum no agreement as to where the blame ought to be laid, or the remedy found for the uafortuo" ate fiasco which has given away the Liberal cause just when a united front should have told with great force on the enemy's position. There is a disposition to blame the press on both sides of the controversy for exaggerating the crisis by inflame' tory comments on the LLOYD-GEORGE diViSioo and this is not without reason. To speak of 50 Imperialist "Schism "is pitching it rather strong, and some journalists write as if they wished to pro- duce:results which should verify their assertion that the Pro-Boors wish to drive the Imperialists out of the party. They have no intention or desire. Sinee they acquired the "Daily News," the anti-war sec- tion has been decidedly aggressive; but they da not aim at more than influencing and perhaPs leading the policy of the party. They complain of the front bench being inactive, and they certainlY have shown no lack of energy; but whether thor heal has been sufficiently tempered by discretion) is a question upon which the occupants of the front bench are not yet satisfied. They have secured the Opposition leader, and now expect the bulk of the Imperialists to fall into line. But the latter look upon this claim as altogether unreasow able, and they hold that quiescence is the 104 that can be expected of them, on a question 130: which divisions have arisen on matters of privet judgment. At the same time they repudiate al° desire ascribed to them by journalistic fiction becoming absorbed bY the Unionist Pert.ii; Neither is there any truth, probablYo the assertion that tho Imperialists threat*: to join the Government in the nest war v°t: and that the extremists intend to give them early opportunity of doing so. tqually impressed with the necessity for unity,but there does not at present exist any sufficiently 'strong moral influence to provide a secure basis. There is undoubtedly a question of which section than lead the party on war topics, and while this %tnpetition lasts there is lbound to be an absence Of those mutual advances and accommodations 173:lic1a might tend to allay feeling on both sides,

niad allow reason and sober judgment to prevail, good deal of the trouble has arisen from the lack of a proper confidential communication be- tween the party managers of the two, sections, Which might have been maintained had a due re- gard been preserved for the right of private judg- zent which is the birthright of every man claim- ing the name of Liberal. Complaint was made When Sir HENRY FOWLER was charged with the

duty of moving the amendment to the Finance that Liberals below the gangway had not been consulted in the selection; and equally, when lir LLOYD GEORGE moved his resolution on the aciugee Camps,that he did so without consultation With the front bench in any shape or form. In such Circumstances it is absurd to expect that by mere force Of party ties such resolutions can command the united support of the party. The most that eau, be expected is that Liberals who cannot take tha view of the movers of resolutions should refrain from lioting against them. Silo want of engineering power, such a lack of party discipline Clearly leave the rank and file of the party free to to according to their convictions or indeed as tbsY may feel inclined. What is most required, and there are indications that the course is con- plated, is that the Liberal Leader should call a rceeting of all sections of the parliamentary party With a view to arriving at a proper understanding as to the lino that is to be taken on all questions bearing upon the war. A certain latitude of action must be left to members who hold extreme "jaws on either side, and this ought to be done Without recrimination. But a large majority of the members ought to be able to find a common basis of action upon which confidence might be restored and something like 'party—dificipliae !aight be possible. Unless this can be done thew is some danger that Government by party may disappear, leaving no choice between a despotic taocracy and the French system of Government tsectl°ll3 which in the Republic has been fraught With Such public disadvantage.

Why Not Tax mining Tan heaviest fall the Gos ornment have had Royalties ? in this Parliament over- took them on Tuesday night, when their majority fell to 28 on the amendment moved by Mr 4010E:sou on the Finance Bill, to provide for the recipients of mining royalties sharing the general barden of war taxation. It has been pointed out Previously in these columns what an excellent °PPortunity the Government have missed of lightening the popular burden by calling in the 1144ing royalties and other forms of unearned in- veinent to the aid of the taxpayer. The division t)1:1 the MoKssire amendment shows how wide- 13I3read is the feeling that the time has now arrived llben the subject should be taken up. It was no 4Ccident. The amendment was down on the PaPer in due form and it was seen that the House /NI working its way towards it, so that the plea !.4 surprise cannot be put forward as an ex- 'll`44stion of the absence of such a large I)er of Government supporters. The 1145w:1:lent no doubt will take the that it has arisen from the laxity that has 784 already shown, and results purely from the ,•_/74r-confidences of a large majority. But if they ,e9ck the trouble to inquire into the cause of this lerity they should find that it arises mainly from the determitlatioa the Government have shown not to be guided by public opinion when it runs eantrary to their pet ideas and party traditions The people's representatives,who,have to face their constituencies, accept those ideas and:traditions. 'or the mostpart in a very modified form, and the Pteposal that the landlord who pockets a tax on "that people's industry should in his turn be taxed So fair and equitable on the face of it that it ' Wati difficult for any man who is amenable to public °Pinion to take a stand against it. Indeed in the Present emergency it was only the most bigoted ieetantiaeirin:f their party, and those who preferred well with their party managers all,other considerations, who ware equal 7 standing by the Government in their `eclhardy opposition to such an equitable thr°P°B4l. in the words of Mr THOMAS SHAW, .snere are three parties to the question of taxation Coal, the royalty owner, who is the real owner, he so-called coal owner, who is only a lessee of ‘go mines, and the labouring man. The last two ilre being taxed, the first escapes. The Chancellor et the Exchequer could not see the point, and °tied out against the injustice of taxing the royalty Which was a fixed sum, when the coal masters had been making millions out of the enhanced prices. %lite true, money has been made by both master d miner, but the big profits and the high wages :11!/13' not continue very long and the tax will be ,411. ere all the same. Again while the master draws 1441_ Profits and the miner his wages, the former 7i given his enterprise, risked his capital, :Plied himself sedulously in a competitive busi- t% to earn his profit, and the latter has given I,„th labour and skill to earn his wages. The t.Z!.lty owner has contributed neither risk, enter- labour, skill, nor application of any kind be- securing his claim on what other men pro- and this is the class the Government in- Upon relieving from the burden which they 411°0 never tired of saying ought to be borne by on classes of the community. Legislation for el:l_4es and administration in the interest of tr7lsfto.,_ as a party policy may be very convenient ' that'a sorce points of view. But there is a Nemesis thqind it. Retribution may be tardy, but it is (I,4re following on behind, and when it finally Yertakes its victims and makes itself felt, the ess— sst will be overwhelming.

i --- 411,004 rather surprising to learn that the power of t° the Rouse of Lords under the Work-

men's Compensation Act slipped into that measure by accident. So many officials examine bills before they are said to be finally " drafted " that any mistake of this sort ought to be avoidable. The right of appeal, as the Lord Chancellor said, has in one sense worked very well in the matter of justice. Some decisions of the High Court on appeal from the County Courts have been wisely reversed. But it would not do to permit such extensive litigation where one of the parties is a poor man. The knowledge that the rich defendant sould:carry hisicaseitope highest tribunal has doubt- less led to many a compromise :disadvantageous to the claimant. Law of this sort is too great a luxury for the lower classes to be able to indulge in it There must be finality earlier. Accordingly,in the new bill dealing with Courts of Appeal this last resort has been stopped. It is an ill wind that blows nobody any good,and so m. important decis- ions, which will serve to interpret the Workmen's Compensation Act so long as it remains in force, have been obtained. They will afford guidance to the judges in the lower courts, and the possibility of a miscarriage of justice is less than it was. The trouble has never been with the evidence, but with the definition of phrases. Most of the diffi- cult ones have now notes of cases attached.

-- Scientific people have long given over using the word" solid" as applied to the earth, or even to that crust of it which supports our habitations, and but rarely now gives indications of being but a film, after all, over a molten mass. The seismo- logist knows that the earth is subject to fits of trembling, and that wave-like movements pass through its substance from time to time. Some experiments,however,which have been lately made in British Columbia reveal a degree of plasticity which had barely been expected. An experi- menter who had invented a particularly delicate instrument for observing minute changes in the earth's substance has actually discovered that the mere fluctuations in the weight of the air as re- vealed by the movements of the mercury in the barometer cause changes of level of the surface. Mr Napier Denison's apparatus' indeed, proved in some respects more Sensitive than the barometer itself, for it indicated the changes of surface pro- I duced by anti-cyclones long beiore they arrived at the spot at which the observations were made, high atmospheric pressure on one side and low at- mospheric pressure on the other causing a tilting, which, slight as it was, of course, was yot to be determined and measured by suitable instru,nonts. Thus we have one more lesson as to the relat;-e- -ness of all our ternap, scientific or otherwise. Terra firma, the solid earth, is, as compared with abso- lute inflexibility—if such a quality of matter is conceivable—the jelly to whiola Darwin in one of his lectures likened it.

Another gratuitous insult for Warrington! In a recently issued cyclists' touring guide we hap- pened upon the following expressive and uncom- plimentary sentence, "once oft the:somewhat ill- kept roads of the ill-smelling town of Warrington the cyclist is sure to enjoy this ride." There now! "111-kept and ill-smelling!" What do Warring- tonians, and particularly those responsible for the Government of the town, think of this candid criticism? It comes rather hard after the improvements already made and those in pros- pect are remembered. " 111-smelling " we cer- tainly take exception to. It is quite evident the compiler of the tourists' guide has never visited the neighbouring towns of Widnes and St Helens or he would not style Warrington an "ill-smelling" place. "111-kept roads" is a soft impeachment we must still admit,though it would be more correct to say streets instead of roads, for the latter have been much improved. But the streets! Take any of the routes right through the town and the cyclist is ensured a violent shaking he will not easily forget. Bridge-street in partic- ular is a nameless horror. The bottom portion contains absolutely the worst piece of sett-paving we ever traversed, and it is no wonder the chance visitor spills ink vindictively when he comes to make notes for the benefit of his fellows. Cannot Warrington clear itself of this standing reproach ?

Seven thousand six hundred signatures to a memorial is not a bad result of a fortnight's can- vassing, and we hope the weight of this petition will not be under-estimated when the bill prohibit- ing the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors to Children under 16 years comes up for Parliamentary sanc- tion. Had the tune available been double what it was it is quite likely that the number of petitioners from Warrington would have been 15,000 instead of 7,600, the canvassers being unable to visit every street in the town as intended. Nevertheless the Band .of Hope Union and other temperance organisations have performed a creditable piece of work, and one too which empha- sises their earnestness in the cause of tem- perance. There is no question that the serving of children at public-houses is a practice fraught with the gravest moral danger to the community. The youngsters who are sent for the dinner or supper beer hear and see things which should be entirely foreign to their tender eyes and ears, and the results in after life are often deplor- able. Scores of cases of intemperance and moral ruin are traceable to the serving of children in the public-house and we are glad to have the testi- mony of the canvassers to the fact that the aver- age intelligent artisan was always quite ready to sign the memorial. It is to be hoped that Mr. Crombie's bill will pass the House.

The united opposition of the riparian autheri- ties to the new Port Sanitary Bill has fallen to pieces. At a conference held at Warrin.gton on Saturday several authorities agreed to combine in opposition to the Bill but they have since backed out and the opposition will be confined to those authorities who will take independent action. The WsrriEgton Corporation is one of the authorities which is determined to oppose the bill and it is probable that Widnes Corporation and Whiston Rural Council will act on similar lines. The Bill will shortly engaae the attention of a committee of the House of Commons and the opponents will then have an opportunity of stat- ing their grievances. The mere fact that Warring- ton and Widnes will have to pay one-thirteenth of the cost of the Port Sanitary Authority without receiving the least compensation from the water- way,is one that ought to weigh with the committee. The Local Government Board seem determined to carry the Bill in spite of all opposition, and it cannot be said that the opponents enter upon their task with great anticipations of success. There is nothing, however, to be lost by trying.
. di., C, L. ,

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
FISHING MATCH AT THE OLD CAN:

The Runcorn Anglers' Association held their opening match at the Old Quay Waters, Runcorn,on Wednesday last. Mr Edwin Starkey, Widnes, was Captain, but the attendance was not very encourag- ing. Atter three hours patient work with rod and line the prizes were awarded as follows :—Mr 8 Bailey, Regent-street,first, 11 ounces (three fish.) Mr George Davies, Widnes, second; and Mr 1' Worrell, Runcorn, third. Sport was considered good for the time of the year,and one fisher secured 29 fish a haul which only weighed 9 ounces.

div.head: RUNCORN PARISH- CHURCII.
div.p: RUNCORN PARISH- CHURCII.

On Sunday special sermons in aid of the National Schools were preached at the above church. Special music was given by the cheir, assisted by a num- ber of children from the schools, these having been most efficiently trained by Mr F R Boraston and the lady teachers. The Rev Canon Maitland Wood occu- pied the pulpit in the morning. He took for his text the words," If my father and my mother for- sake ma the Lord taketh me up." In the afternoon a flower servile was conducted by the Rev and lion C F Cross vicar of Stratton, who also preached at night. A large number of flowers were presented, to be afterwards distributed among the sick of the town. The children also participated in the even- ing service, and on the whole, the singing was well balanced, and reflected great credit on the con- ductor, Mr F R Boraston. The collections realized a fair amount.

NARROW -661P8 FROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN, On Monday afternoon, a lad of fourteen, named Ralph Riley, Speakman-street, employed by Mr Hewitt, ship chandler, had a very narrow escape from drowning in one of the docks at Weston Point. The boy bad been sent by his master to a flat" The Maggie" lying in the river Weaver with a load of potatoes which he was trundling along on a small truck. As he was passing over the qaay side he:had the misfortune to catch the truck wheel against one of the big cranes stretching across the wharf, and fell into the water. Two flatmen heard the splash and subsequent cries and ran to the spot armed with boat hooks with which they fished the unfortunate lad out. After drying his clothes at the navvies hut the lad proceeded on his journey little the worse for his adventure, though doubtless had help not been at hand he would have been drowned.

A DAY IN DELAMERE FOREST. The members of Mr Simister's select class, Bruns- wick School, accompanied by their wives and lady friends, held their first annual picnic on Saturday, when a visit was paid to Delamere Forest in wag- gonettes. The party left Messrs Booth and Son's premises at 2 o'clock, and drove by way of Halton, Frodsham, Kingsley, and Norley. On arrival at Forest View, a capital tea was served, and subse- quently some time was spent in exploring the forest and visiting the lake. Following this there were games, singing, &c, several selections being rendered by the members of the Male Voice Choir. Group photographs of the party were taken by Mr J Newell. Despite the unfavourable climatic con- ditions an enjoyable time was spent. A start for home was made at nine o'clock, Runcorn being reached about 11 p.m.

RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. The half-yearly meeting of, the above organiza- tion was held in the Greeuway-road schoolroom on Saturday evening. The president (fr Thomas Heesom) occupied the chair, and there was a good , attendance of officers and members. After discus- sion it was decided to hold a demonstration in I August. The officers for the ensuing six months were elected as follows .—President, Ur Thomas Heesom ; associate, Mr Alfred Nodenl financial secretaries, Messrs James Johnson and Thos. Dutton; conductors, Messrs George Powell and Edgar Wil- kinson; sentinels, Messrs J T Fowldes and Thos, Barker treasurer, Mr Daniel Bisbrown ; recording secretary, Mr T J Holt ; chaplain, Mr Samuel Tom- linson; auditors, Messrs A Noden and G Powell; sick visitors, Messrs Thomas Clarke,and Edward Key ; patron and treasurer of cadets, Mr T R Whyte; secretary, Mr E W Key. The following were ap- pointed representatives to the Grand Division meeting to be held at Weston in July. Messrs T Cooke, E Rey, T Clarke,T Dutton, and S Tomlinson. An interesting meeting then closed. " SAL?: FIGHT ON RUNCORN HILL" On Friday evening the F and G Companies of the 2nd V.B.C.R. (forming the Runcorn detach- ment) marched to Runcorn Hill. for attack and defence practice. The members of the cyclists' section, being the weaker side, took up a defensive Iposition in the quarries, and the remainder of the detachment, number about 50, formed the attack- ing force. Captains Timmins was in com- mand of the attacking force and Sergeant Phoinix had charge of the defenders, while Captain Ashton acted as umpire. The defenders used great judgment in the positions they occupied, and, on the whole, appeared to have la good idea of what would be required in actual warfare. The practice was most instructive to all ranks. After the return to the Drill Hall Captain Ashton complimented the men on their display. He said the defenders, owing to their small num- bers, left one flank open, which might have been surrounded. On the whole, however, their part wasovery well done. A LAZY MAN PUNISHED. At the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday, before Mr E liaison, Joseph Rowson was charged with absconding from Dutton Workhouse with clothing belonging to the Guardians.—P.C. Shaw stated that in consequence of complaints he received, he went to prisoner's mother's house in High-street, Run- corn, and found the prisoner there. He gave no explanation as to when and why he left the Work- house. Witness subsequently took him to Dr McDougall, who, after examining him, said he was all right mentally, but seine punishment would do him good.—Superintendent Pearson said the prisoner was a nuisance to his mother but she I " fadded " him, and brought him dainty bits to the Police Station.—John Roberts, assistant master at the Workhouse, said the prisoner was very lazy. The other day they put him to work with, an old man 70 years of age, and prisoner said he could not do the work. Witness took him to the doctor, and he told him that there was nothing the matter with him,—ln reply to Mr Imison.witness said that before an inmate could leave the Workhouse he had to give 48 hours' notice. On receipt of the notice pri.ocier would be supplied with his own clothing, with which he entered the house. The prisoner had run away on a previous occasion. His had been in the Army.—Superintendent Pearson said prisoner deserted from the Army, and was discharged with ignominy. Ile had undergone a month's imprison- ment for assaulting his mother.—The witness Roberts said prisoner had been under special obser- vation in the hospital, and witness took him to the doctor last Wednesday week. The doctor said he was perfectly sane; In witness's opinion there was nothing the matter with him except laziness.—The magistrate vmmitted the prisoner to gaol for 7 days' hard labour, and advised him when he came out t 3 abide by the rules of the Workhouse. A TKIP TO BLACKPOOL.

Messrs. William Gossage and Sons, Ltd., Widnes, (of soap renown), on Saturday last afforded their employees their annual trip ; about 1,000 Imrk- people being provided with tickets and bonuses to enable them to enjoy a day's outing at Blackpool. Each man in the employ of the firm received two tickets and Is 6d for dinner; and each boy one ticket and a shilling for dinner. Capital arrange- ments had been made, and some 2,000 people left Widnes (1,. and N.W. Railway) Station in three special trains, at 6.50, 7 and 7.10 a.m. on Saturday morning, reaching Blackpool about two hours later. The Tower and grounds, Big Wheel, Alhambra, promenades, piers, Winter Gardens and other attractions of the seaside town were each in turn visited. Sea voyages and sea baths were partaken of, and up to about 4 30 p.m. most of the company enjoyed themselves in the open air inhaling the pure atmo,phere to their hearts' content. At that hour, however, rain commenced to fall, and 'everyone was driven within doors. This was, of course, disappointing to those who had been un- wise enough to spend their forenoon under cover, in the Tower and Alhambra; but, those who had begun their enjoyment in the open first, had the latter to fall back on, and took the rain as a matter of course. The return journey was made from Talbot-road Station, by trains at 8.16, 8.24 and 840 p.m. respectively, En route train No 1 was over- hauled by No 2, and an interesting race ensued Both parties of trippers leaned out of the windows with speculative interest, and a roar was sent up by the occupants of No 2 as they overhauled No I. This burst of applause was, however, easily Ecl psied when No 1 came sailing by. and practically lef" No 2 standing still. though the latter was making about 45 miles an hour. The incident occurred on the double set of metals just outside Wigan. Widnes was reached by all three trains shortly after ten everybody having enjoyed them- selves without mishap, 1

div.head: WESTON WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: WESTON WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

In connection with the men's bible class an open meeting was held on Sunday, at which a thought- ful address on the subject of conversion was given by Mrs Eyre, of Runcorn. Mr II Dodd presided, and Miss Savage gave an effective rendering of the solo "Remember me." The meeting was well attended by members and friends.

div.head: •• DEATH FROM BLOOD-POISONING AT WIDNES.
div.p: •• DEATH FROM BLOOD-POISONING AT WIDNES.

_ On Friday, at the Clap Gate Hotel, before Mr Brighouse, county coroner, an inquest was held touching the death of John Turton, 57 years, 17, Bale Bank-terrace, Hale Bank, who died on the 19th inst. The evidence showed that deceased was making a canvas bag when he pricked his arm with the needle which did not make it bleed. He was attended by Dr Hutchinson, blood-poisoning ensu- ing. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY A CORRESPONDENT.] Without in any way reflecting upon the Librarian, it is my wish to draw attention to the reprehensible practice exercised more especially by members of the Council and members of the Library Committee,ollborrowing:books:without con- forming to the rules and regulations. Too many gentlemen are at present in the habit of " calling at the window" without their cards. This would not be so disastrous if their forgetfulness ended there, but occasionally all trace of a book is lost, or the public are vainly obliged to a.k for a volume which, instead of being at their disposal, too often lies idle upon the shelf of one who should be the last to allow such a thing to happen.

The Runcorn Free Church Council ha i sounded the first note in the forthcoming school board cam- paign, and on Tuesday next a lecture will be de- livered in the Bethesda Schoolroom, by the Rev J Hirst Hollowell, on the "Education 9uestion." Sir J T Brunner, Bart, M P, will preside, and will be supported by the President of the Cmincil (the Rev A Wells), aaveral members of the School Board, and other gentlemen. The Runcorn public will do well to attend the meeting as at the present time there is no more interesting question before the public than that of education.

Tie visit of the Rev E Lloyd Jones (Manchester) to Runcorn, though but short, will live in our recol- lection for a considerable time ; if for no other reason, for the very important ono that he inspired the Wesleyans of the district with a new sense of their importance, dignity, and responsibility as a political as well as a religious body. The worthy superintendent (the Rev A Wells) ever since his ad- vent in the circuit has upheld the hohour and prestige of his Church in a degree to be admired,as instance his attitude in the matter of the Memorial Service and the Free Church Council, and now the Rev E Lloyd Jones has so emphatically, though un- wittingly endorsed nis conduct, perchance the members of his flock will be more enthusiastic in their support.

Oa Thursday the Ruucorn Urban District Council are said to nave ratified the brhige loan with the Ecclesiastical Commissioners,and the annual repay- I meat of principal and interest is to be £549 103.101 I How does this contrast with what Mr W Handley has said on the subject ? Mr Handley, certainly, has argued they would do well if the town was able to borrow at 3i per cent. But, even when. he made that statement, he pointed out that the cost of re payment would be slightly under a3l rate. Still, he was not satisfied, and advised the townspeople to call it 31. His calculation is now borne out very rem irkably, for the amount just figures out at less than 31 in the Z.

The Council also,l hear, aPpointed Lr R U Pos- nett, the town's director on the Widnes and Ilan- wen Bridge Co., board of directors. lie will bold the office, on behalf of the Town for 3 years and be subject to re-election. Mr S Taylor was first asked to accept the honour,but declined. As an indication of how the Bridge is progressing it may be as wall to state that the plans submitted to the Council, at their committee meeting, were the same as those drawn up for the contracts. We may now look confidently to a definite announcement of the start- ing of operations, and probably will hear some- thing from Sir John Brunner when he visits us on Tuesday.

Just at present there is a deadlock in the matter of the Runcorn Volunteer Band and the Commanders of the Corps. Everyone is talking about it, and in doing so doing very little good. I would advise the refractory ones to reflect on their conduct, and even if they have to " climb down " a bit to do so handsomely, for their o ma ,zood and the good of the town. The many good turns their commanders have done them deserve better recognition ; and, besideS, it is poor policy " cutting the nose off to spite the face."

div.head: --•--- RUNCORN, THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY. AND THE POT TERIES.
div.p: --•--- RUNCORN, THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY. AND THE POT TERIES.
- Mr. Bythell's Bombshell.

When Mr Bythell, (linkman of the Ship Canal Com- pany, at the last meeting of the shareholders indicated in unmistakable terms the possibility of thel company ceasing to be carriers and converting the Bridgwater Canal into a toll-paying waterway and Runcorn docks into a rent-earning unfer-1 taking, considerable consternation was crested amongst the pottery trade of Staffordshire and the shipping community of Runcorn. For nearly a century the Bridgewater Canal, via Ruaeorn, has been the chief route for raw materials for the Potteries, and the execution of Mr. Bythelra threat meant a revolution in the carrying trade. Without loss of time the North Stafford Chamber of Commerce discussed the question. and on the suggestion of the president, Mr E V Greatbatch, the members determined to take a trip to Runcorn, see the accommodation of the docks there,and witness the system of working the traffic for the Potteries. This visit was paid on Wednesday. Every section of the pottery trade and every district is the Potteries was represented ; and there were also included in the party of about 80 bard-beaded business men, ten members of the North Staffordshire Mining Aesocittion, and repre- sentatives of several canal carrying cmcerns,including Messrs LI B ' obbington Stoke, and D Danain T. Runcorn (representing the Anderton Co.) ; Stssirs C V Walker, Stoke, and 0 Ditchfield, Runcorn (Messrs Potter and Sons) ; and Messrs T Foster, Runcorn, and fa beckbeart, Stoke (represented the Salt Iloion). On arrival at Runcorn, Mr John Maclosvcroft, the local agent of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, took the visitors over Runcorn docks, which are about 37 acres in extent, fully two-thirds of which are wharves, sheds and warehouses. Alter luncheon, Mr E V Grestbatcb, president of the Chamber of Commerce, said that Mr Bythell kindly met himself and the executive of the Chamber, and dis- cussed the matter very freely, and stated that what he had said was somewhat In the nature of a feeler but if the trade became more demanding in its require- ments, and the workmen at Runclrn Docks became more difficult to seal with then this Ship Canal Company in all human probability would cease to be canal carriers and become simply toll receivers. In conse- quence, the members of the Chamber of Com- merce were that day attempting some solu- tion of the difficulty by viewing the pro- visions and inspecting the arrangements made for the water carriage of materials to North Stafford. They bad Seen Runcorn Docks, which were specially laid out for the purposes of pottery work, and also Weston Point and Ellesmere Port. They had seen the arrange menus made for the trade of North Stafford, and he ventured to say that so far as Runcorn was concerned it was specially adapted and especially Jar d out for the service of the Staffordshire potters. (Rear, he" )

div.head: "OLD BRUNSWICK" SUNDAY SCHOOL. --- 101st Anniversary.
div.p: "OLD BRUNSWICK" SUNDAY SCHOOL. --- 101st Anniversary.

The members of the "Old Brunswick "Sunday schools, Runcorn, on Sunday, put for ward their best efforts to cosecs the 101st anniversary of this thriving Nonconformist Sunday school an unqualified success,and succeeded, too, in a measure gratifying in the extreme. Failing Mr Watkinson,the services of Mr E Lloyd Jones, Menchester,had been obtained,as preacher and lecturer; and, as if to suit the occesi JO, the large congregation who assembled in the morning were told :—" And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God," (Romans viii 28), a text upon which the preacher founded a most helpful discourse, illustratieg how the teat was the most original and helpful contri- bution to Christian life and thought. In the evening, whilst expeunding the lessons, tbe Rev E Lloyd Jones said :—For the last quarter of a century the uppermost question in the minds of all earnest Christians: had been " What is the relicion of the Old Testament to the New ; to what extent, if any, is the Old Testament a guide to the Christian's life ?" All the most capable men had answered that the 0:d Testament was not a guide to the Christian's life. It was utterly inadequate, if not misleading. The question of the day was how to bring over what was called the Christian mind from the Old Testament point of view Co the New Testament point of view ? Ile could under- stand the attachment of many good people to the Old Testament as a rule of life, for it was so much easier to be an Old Testament Saint than a New Testament Chris- tian. If they wanted to believe in war, to kill anyone who was in their wae ; to be immoral in the borne life, and hold many other such views there was plenty of illustrations in support thereof to he felled in the old Testament. He believed in the "sermon on the Mount," and when people were brought face to face with the beauties of that they did not like it. The sermon, at the same service, was founded on Luke ix, 28, " lietook Peter, James and John up to the mountain to pray" In the course of his remarks he said that the immediate object of Christ was not the education of the Jewish nation, but the education of twelve men. He selected twelve men to go with Him wherever He went, to hear all His sermons, to see all His miracles, and to follow Him for the three years of His ministry. It Was Only in the third year that death was male the condition of salvation, and there were a number of things in the second year which were not to be found in the first. Successful religions teaching necessarily had its roots in the death of Christ, and the reason why much of the cultured teaching of the present day failed to attract the masses was because it dwelt on Christ the genius, and not on Christ the Saviour. LECTURE ON "THE PILGRIM'S PROGRESS." The Rev E Lloyd Jones delivered his popular lecture entitled "The Pilgrim's Progress "in St. Paul's Church on Monday evening. Mr R El Posnett presided, and besides the lecturer there were on the platform :—Revs. Alfred Wells (superintendent minister), J B Forster, S Wright. Messrs S Taylor, F J Norman, A R Nnrman, E Guest, J R Frith, J Mason Frith, Rewlinsoe, G Bellamy, T Boote, J W Baguley and L Rosenberg. Toe Chairman said during the past year they had seen unexampled prosperity in the Runcorn circuit in the building and enlargement of Sunday schools. It had been a jeer to everyone. Their hearts had rejsiced in the fact that they had been ebb e during the past twelve months to:tiring a larger number of childrenlthan they had done before within the teaching of evangelical truth, Methodist doctrine, and to the knowledge of the love of Jesus Christ. One thing he had noticed In con- nection with the extension of their Sunday school was that wherever they had provided better accommodation for the children it had had a reflex action upon the church. Wherever they had improved the Sunday school accommodation, and brought more children into the schools, and made them brighter and better, they had indirectly added an enormous influence upon their church life. If they took for example Weston Point they found they had put up a new school and provided ac- commodation for twice as many children as they had before. They found it was not full, and the number of people who attended their services had largely increased. That was one feature that they could greatly rejoice in. It proved this fact, that if they cared for the children they were caring at the same time for their Church. That was true all along the line. The children were havinz a far better chance in the schools, and they would find it would have a wonderful effect on their church life, because where the children went, and learned to love tkeir Saviour, they would bring their parents after them. They should let their children see their absolute loyalty and devotion to the church of their choice. There were possibly tempts- rions wnich came in their way to cause them perhaps to discard their Methodism, or occasionally to act a little frivolously, but if they were to /thew their children what real loyalty to their church meant they must let them understand that they were intensely in earnest themselves. (Hear, hear.) He felt very anxious to impress upon the boys and girls present that Methodism was the grandest Church in the world. (Applause.) ' There was no sphere anywhere in the world where they could serve God as he believed they could there. They could do a great service for the Master in Methodism. There was work for all of them, if only they would show their loyalty and wiliingnees etc, do their best. There was no man prouder of the Church, and no man who loved the Church more than the one who was actively engaged in its work. (A oplause.) The Lecturer said it was over 200 years since John Bunyan fiehrhed his earthly pilgrimage, He was born in 1628 and died in 1688, and that made him a man of 80 Re was 50 years of,age when he wrote" The Pilgrim's Progress," He (the lecturer) always considered that those 60 years were the most remarkable in the history of this country—the most remarkable in thst it pleased God to give to this country a larger number of great men than He ever gave either before or after in any similar period. The Puritan period was the most un- usual and fruitful harvest of real brains this country ever saw. Writers of history would hear him out when he said this. The method of Providence in giving great men had always been to give them in clusters. At one period there was an abundance of great men • at another there were absolutely none. Without maligning the most characteristic features of the times in which they lived, he would say that this was the day of small men. He did not know a pre-eminently great man anywhere Let them go back 40 years ago, and they found Carlyle, Emerson, Venda!, Huxleseßuekin,Tennyson,Martineau, Browning, Gladstone. Who was left but Rudyard Kip- ling and the absentoninded beggar ? Who could measure the distance from the brain of Thomas Carlyle and the brain of Rudyard Kipling ? Pre- eminently great men did not live in this country to-day. But the fact that Bunyan WAS surrounded by such great Contemporaries was no advantage to him. Be ceuld not identify a single thought that be borrowed from any of then:elle could sot spot a single illustration that Ihe ever borrowed from them Mever there was an original man that man was John Banyan, and if ever there was an original book it was "The Pilgrim's Progress." Was it possible to explain the unparalleled and the norivalled magnetism of" The Pilgrim's Progress " How was it that it was the most popular book that had ever been written by an Englishman ? He could not • point to one feature and say that is the height of his strength ; that is the secret of his power. No. There were at least balf-a-dozen features whir% contributed their quota. When be had named his half-a-dozen pilgrims others would be able to start half-a-dozen more 11 on their own account. He would name the features Ithat appealed to hirn.First of stilt was's religious book. That stood for a groat deal. Whenever they read " The I Pilgrim's Progress" they never felt that Bianyan was thinking at second band or describing at second hand.lle (the lecturer) did not think it was difscult to differenti- ate between a book that was an echo and real thoughts. This was the secret of the originality of Bunyan. He was not expressing a thing thet his eyes had not seen, his hands had not handlerlor his own experience lead not read. The style of the book counted for a great deal. " The Pilgrim's Progress" was a novel, and thousands of persons who had objected to a novel had said their prayers over this book many a time. Another feature was that the book was undenominational. He defied any man to say it was written by a Baptist. All the great books were written for humanity and not for a sect. Of course, Bunyan was a Baptist, but they could not discover it. The early Baptists were very much annoyed that he did not put more water in the book. (Laughter.) It was glorious for Johnißunyan the Bap- tist, to take every pilgrim to glory without' dipping any; of them- If John Bunyan had dipped his pilgrim it would have stepped his progress (Laughter.) There were 200 characters in the book. They were not all fully described, and they were not all men, but they all exhibited the genius of Bunyan as photographer of character. If they went through " The Pilgrim's Progress " they would find something that the old race of Methodist preachers never saw. If they remembered, the old Methodist preacher had only one station from which to start his pilgrims to glory— that was the City of Destruction—and he ran the train straight through from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, and passed thousands of villages, and un- less the villagers went to the City of Dastrtsction they could never take a ticket. Bunyan provided a station at every village. Some started from the Town of Vain- glory, others from Vanity Fair, but the majorityotarted from the City of Destruction. The reason for the great charm of" The Pilgrim's Progress " was the wonderful care that was taken of week pilgrims. It was a book Pre-eminently suited for weak pilgrims, and for that reason he thought it was all the better for strong O- rin". His (the lecturer's) ideal preacher was not the man who conveyed the greatest amount of light into dark minds, but the man who imparted the great- est amount of force into feeble wills—the man who by the magnetism of his sympathy could give new strength to the feeble will. He declared that the human race suffered more from weakness of will than from obduracy of conscience. The most cruel men be had ever known were the men who could never stand and never speak except with sneers and contempt for those who were weak. After dealing with the characters of Christian, Faithful, and Hopeful, the lecturer said that notwith- s books, b e eh , great char= and popularity of thehtg were four objections taken to it by its critics. The first was that " The Pilgrim's Progress "

'could not be a religious book for all ages, because it made religion too doleful and forbidding. It called the Christian life a pilgrimage. The twentieth century pre- ferred excursions. It was a religious excursion that was most popular. The great cry of the age from the young men and young women was • Can you make religion easy, can you make it pleasant, cheap ? Can't you drop the pilgrimage and give us an excursion, first class, free tickets, victuals provided, and an assurance that we come back at ten ?" They knew they could not. The conflict with sin could not be done oa excursion lines. Objection was taken to •• The Pilgrim's Pro- gress " because it was a Puritan book. It was described as that aipect of religion that would not go down in the West Ead, but might possibly suit the East There were ministers in " The Pilgrim's Progress," but there were no clerics. Jesus Gloria did not make ' doctrine he condition 'lf salvation. The difficulty in religion was not i g tting it but in giving it. (Applause.) The lecturer illustrated the points et his lecture with many striking incidents in his own experi- I cane, and at the close he received an oration. I

Or; the motion of Mr T Simister, seconded by Mr A R Norman, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr Jones for his lecture and services on Sunday. The Rev E Lloyd Jones responded. The following scholars received early attendance certificatcs :—Girls : Kizia Whyte, Lizzie Tickle,Mabel ' Fazackerley, Elizabeth McCutcheon, Elsie Tickle, Jessie Stubbs, Hannah Tickle, Lucy Norbar3 , Lizzie Holt. Boys : Alfred Lea,Ern. at Lawton, Eigar Lawtan,John Saunders, George Saunders, James Lea, John Tickle Samuel Pickstock, William Henry Whyte, Leonard Whyte, Harry Cox. The meeting then terminated with the singing of the Doxology and Benediction.

TZE The musical portion ot the services was, as usual, a feature ia itself. Indeed in heartiness and effectivehess the equal from a congregational point cf view could only be met with in Yorkshire or Wales. Mr Birkett was responsible for the training of the children, and the choir (was under the conductorship of Mr R Morris. The best rendered item was the general hymn, " Come, let us with our Lord arise," sing to (Celestie Urbs), which far surpassed the special hymns. Of the latter " The hidden life," " The song of the standard," " The Angels' anthem," and" Now the day is over," were well rendered, the collections throughout the anniversary realizA £7O. The scholars number 500 sad the staff 60.

div.head: WIDNES FOOTBALLtCLUB.
div.p: WIDNES FOOTBALLtCLUB.
Annual Meeting.
The annual meeting of the Widnes Football Club was held on Wednesday evening, Mr H Wade Daacon in the chair.
A SERIOUS FINANCIAL POSITION.

The balance sheet was read by the retiring secretary Mr McNJrton, and showed that there was a debit bal- ance for the Reason of £343 Cs id, the total expenditure being £1,278 16+ lid and the iIICOMB £935 3s sd. The principal items of expenditure were :—Outstanding accounts £159 Os 7d; lost time to players and trainers, £374 73 4d ; hotel expenditure, £139 163 3.1. The chief sources of income were :—First and second team gate money £432 2s ; Nirthern Union and S. W. Lancashire cup competition, £209 Bs 4d ; works competition gate money, £56 lOs 11 ; subscriptions and donations, £lO2 16s 6d.

The Chairman said there was one point to which attention should be drawn, and that was the serious financial position which the club fund itself in. Last year there was a debit balance of £l5B. This year it had been increased to £343. so that roughly speaking the club was £2OO worse off than this time last year. To one who did net know the inner working of the club it seemed absolutely necessary for the management to do something to reduce the very large debit balance. He did not profess to know how it could be done, but it was obviously a matter for careful consideration. So far as one could judge football clubs seemed to be run as business concerns and they should be run to pay. lie hoped the committee wou!d keep this in mind. The report was adopted. BLECTIJN OF OFFICER 9, _ . _ _

On the proposal of Councillor Laws, seconded by Mr Smith, the President (Mr H Wade Deacon) was duly 1-elected, and Colonel Hall Walker was added to the list of vice-presidents. The following gentlemen were also elected :—Mr F W Smith, secretary; G S Bown, captain first team ; T Peacock, sub-captain ; J H captain A team ; M Wickham,sub-captain; F W Wright, treasurer ; J C Evans, financial secretary. The only change in the committee was the non-election of Coun- cillor C Hemingway. the successful candidates being Councillor T Law' 61 votes ; Messrs T Minton, 59 ; E Goodon, 56 • J nSmith, 51 ; D Brennan, 49 ; J Barber, 48; A Critchley, 48 ; J E Farrell, 41. Mr Cristie said he would like to know on behalf of the members what were the club's prospects for the coming season with regard to the new league in the Lancashire Senior Competition. Mr Smith, on behalf of the Committee, said he could not tcll them any more than had appeared in the public press. He could not go into the manner in which the clubs had formed the new league, but what they pro- posed to do in Lancashire, as an alternative measure, was to reconstruct the Lancashire Senior Competition and take five new clubs In, They would lose something by the better clubs being with drawn, and they would also lose by having heavier expenses to meet when they went away. It was also proposed to convert the present West Lancashire com- petition into a league to take in six clubs, Widnes, St. Helens, Warrington, Runcorn, Wigan and Leigh. They would thus get their local fixtures between Runcorn and Warrington, although only in a league of second importance. Whether the club would suffer remained to be seen. It remained for the members to say whether they would support the club which only bad second class football.
On the proposition of Councillor C Hemingway, aeconded by tar Farrell, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, to which he sui:ably responded.

div.head: FOOTBALL. -- Lancashire Senior Competition.
div.p: FOOTBALL. -- Lancashire Senior Competition.

There was a meeting of the clubs comprising this competition at Manchester on Tuesday nigh. Previous to the proceedings commencing, Mr Fred. Wright was elected as representative of the Widnes Club, in place of Mr E BPSorton. who has given up the secretaryship of that club. It was expected that the resignations of Salford, Swinton, Broughton Rangers, Oldham, War- rington, Itunenn and Leigh would be formally ten- dered; but this will be deferred until the minutes of the last meeting of the General Committee of the North- ern Union have been confirmed at the next monthly meeting, to be held in Manchester on the first Tuesday in July. HOMING.

div.head: Runcorn Society.
div.p: Runcorn Society.

The society flew their fifth old-bird race from Jersey on Saturday, distance 229 miles. The birds were liberated by Mr Ashton, Liverpool and District Federa- tion convoyer, at 85a m, wind south-east, clear. The , following velocities per minu'e were attained Edwards, 1,285 yards ; Marshall, 1,214; Killcross, 1.178; I Dunbavin, 1,085 ; Howard, 1,050; Shaw and Son, 1,009* I Dixon and Cobb, 927. Mr Edwards wins 61r Guy's special of a pair of squakers, and Mr Dunbavin wins Mr Davies's special of. a pair of squeakers for best averaee old-bird races. The Mid-Cheshire Federation, On Saturday a meeting of the Mid-Cheshire Homing Federation was held at the Lion Flotel,Knutsford. There were representatives present from the various clubs. The question of the Worcester race, on May 11th, was brought up for consideration. It was stated that five baskets of birds from Sandbach wee not liberated until several minutes after the others. It was decided to declare the race a federation race, and to refund Sand bach their fees. The Jersey race on the previous Monday was next cons'dered. The race, it was stated, proved a very disastrous one, three-fourths of the birds not having returned. The convoyer wrote stating that some birds out of two or three baskets were missing evidently having been stolen, some twigs on the sides having been cut away. The race was declared a federa- tion race.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE MAGISTRATES' CLERK AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF THE MAGIS- TRATES' CLERK AT WARRINGTON.

After fulfilling the duties of Clerk to the War- rington Borough Magistrates for a period of thirty- three years,Mr H B White has resigned the position. The magistrates accepted his resignation on Tuesday afternoon, when a meeting to consider. the matter was held at the Town Hall under the presidency of the Mayor. At the came meeting Mr II B White's son, Mr George F F White, who has occupied the position of deputy Clerk for a number of years, was unanimously appointed to succeed his father in the office of Clerk at a salary of £5OO per annum. Mr FL B White was appointed magistrates' clerk in 1868 and Mr G F F White has assisted his father in the office since his admission as a solicitor in 1884. In 18S6 he was formally appointed deputy clerk by his father with the sanction of the magistrates. Mr R B White's salary was fixed by the Council at .£5OO per annum in February, 1885. The appointment of Mr G F F White to the position will give the utmost satisfaction to all who have duties to perform in connection with the business of the County Borough Police Court. Mr White has seldom been absent from a sitting of the Court and hiecourteous manner and genial personality have won for him many friends.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. The Rev. J. T. Schofield's Farewell
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. The Rev. J. T. Schofield's Farewell
Sermons.

On Sunday lait the lity J T Schofield, who is about to take up the pastorate of North-street Baptist Church, Leeds,concluded his ministry at Golbornc-street Church, Warringten. There were good congregations especially at the evening service. In the morning Mr Schofield addressed his sermon more especially to his deacons and churchworkers,whilst at the cvening service he preached upon the words "For I determine IlOt to know anything among 3, ou, save Jesus Christ, and Him Crucified." These are the words upon which he based his first ser- mon at Golborne-streer. He said he should like to finish at the point where he commenced—at tus Cross. As they were reminded on Tlaursday,the first sermon he preached after settling in Warrington was upon that text and now as he closed his ministry, he desired to bring back to their memories that one central theme in the Gospel. When he commenced his work his purpose was to try to build up a church. He wished them to be a liberal, generous, self-sacrificing and independent church. He had endeav- tired to make them feel as far as he could, that all they did in connection with church work should be done for Christ and Him Crucified. He was not sorry now that he took up that position. Mr Schofield, in conclusion, exhorted all his friends to give themselves to Jesus Christ. After the Benediction bad been pronounced the choir and the congregation sang " God be with you till we meet again,"and Mr Schofield was wished" God speed " by the members of the con- grgation as they left the church.

Clirist Church Enlargement Scheme. The largely increasing congregation at Christ Church, Latchford has made further accommodation urgently necessary. An enlargement scheme was formulated some time ago and approved. It was provided for the erection of a north aisle,!contairung seating accommoda- tion for over 100 persons. The plans were in due course pasEed.and it was expected that the work would be com- menced early this year, but owing to monetary and other difficulties the carrying out of the scheme has had to be postponed.-.-The '• Christ Church Magazine," for June contains the following reference to the scheme : " We fear that it will be a great disappointment to our friends to know that the work of enlarging the church is not to be commenced till next February. In the fret place many of our committee were strongly of opinion that we ought to have more 'money before embarking on PO considerable an 7undertaking, and in the second place the church societies from whom we expect assistance make it an abselute rule not to make grants unless the plans have Iren submitted to and approved by their committees b?fore the work is commenced. To wait until thd committees of these societies had met and approved our plans would have delayed our beginning the work till early in August and it would have been going on all through the winter. There was therefore . no course open to our committee but either to sacrifirie any hope of help from the church societies or to abandon the work for the present: Needless to say we chose the latter course, and have delayed our building operations till next February. We have nad paid or promised to the Church Enlargement Fund £9lO, but as the treasurer is away we are unfortunately not able to print a further list of names and amounts. This will be done in the nert magazine. A good deal more mon.!y is wanted—perhaps £4oo—and with a view to assist in raising this the Church-workers' Association are think ing of holding a two days' bazaar in the Parish Roma early in December. We hope all our friends will give this effort ready and hearty assistance."

div.head: GRAPPENHALL
div.p: GRAPPENHALL

Pamir Cocrlicm.—Tuesday evening's meeting of this Council, which was one of the shortest on record, was presided over by Mr J Charlton Parr. There was also present Messrs Thomas Smith, F Ellison, L James, T Chamberlain, and A Lister Kaye.—The chairman and Mr Kaye signed the usual declaration of acceptance of office. The clerk seated that at the last meeting a com- mittee was appointed with respect to several street improvements which were required. The Surveyor to the Rural Council had been informed in the matter and most of the improvements had been carried out —The:Chairman said he had received a communication from the Clerk of the Peace with re;pect to the proposed memorial to the late Queen Victoria. In the letter it was stated that the subscriptions already received for:the National Memorial (Lord Mayor of London's fund) amounted to £343, and for the Clunty Memorial, £l7B 14s 65;making,a total sum of £521 14s 6d contributed by inhabitants of Cheslaire.The hope:wag expressed that the co-operation of that Council might be relied upon in bringing the matter under the notice of the inhabitants of the parish with a view to further subscriptions.

div.head: PROPOSED WARRINGTON TRAMWAYS.
div.p: THE PROPOSED WARRINGTON TRAMWAYS.
The Board of Trade's Decision.

On Wednesday, the Town Clerk of Warrington (Mt .1 Lyon Whittle) received a communication from the Board of Trade sanctioninx the application of the Coy. potation to borrow £83,050 br tramway purposes. The scheme includes the construction of electric tramways from the centre of the town to Baukey Bridges, Latch- ford and Stockton Heath and the provisions of a car shed and repairing shop ou the site of the old gas works in Mersey-street. It will be remembered that at a recent inquiry, Mr Langdon, barrister, who appeared for Mr Adam Horrocks questioned the right of the Corporation to construct a line along Mersey. street in order that the empty cars might be stabled at the Old Gas Works, on the ground that the Corporation ' had not widened the street to the stipulated width. The Board of Trade, in their decision, accept the ex- planation given on behalf of the Corporation, hat this tra-n line is only to be used for the conveyance of empty cars to the shed, and that in the event of it being used for passenger traffio the widenings will be made.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

SHOCKING TRAM ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS. Mr Fred W Fidler, of St Helens, met with a horrible death ma Wednesday night in Prcscot-road, St Helene. Mr Fidler was a chemical engineer, and lived for many years at Knowsley-road, but has for some time lodged at 3, Catham-street, St Helens. About a quarter-past eleven last night he was walking down Prescot-road to return to St Miens, and when near the top of Boundary- road crossed the road, evidently with the intention of boarding one of the electric cars proceeding to St Helen. By some means or ether Mr Fidler was knocked down, and although the car was fitted with a liNuard, be ot under the wheels, which passed over him. Ile waS carried for some distance under the car, and almost an hour elapsed before he could be extricated. It was then found that ,Mr Fidler's legs were broken, his body mangled, and hie head shockingly injured, death having been almost instantaneous. Deceased was about forty years of age, and one of the best known townsman of St Helens, where he was most highly respected. The body was removed to the mortuary. The affair caused a great sensation in the neighbourhood.

DOUBLE DAILY SERVICE TO THE ISLE OF MIN.—Com• mencing Monday next, July 1, the Isle of Man Steam Packet Co. will run their double daily service between Liverpool and the Isle of Man, and vice versa, thus affording splendid facilities for visitors to the Island. Every day except Sundays boats will leave Liverpool Landing-stage at 10 30 a.m and 2 p.m. (Saturdays 5 p.m. and 12.30 night), arid from Douglas 9 a.m. and 4 pm. (also 12.30 a.m. Monday-Sunday night.) From the 29th June excursions will became daily, boats leav- ing Liverpool at 10.30 a.m., arriving attlouglas 2 p.m.. leaving Douglas 4 p.m., and arriving Liverpool again. 7.45. Excursions are also run from Fleetwood and Douglas and back, every day from June 29: Day excur- sions are also run from Douglas to Glasgow, to enable visitors to see the exhibition, while for those who desire something more, information can be obtained in the company's handbook (free),of the !railings to Belfast, Glasgow, Dublin, round the island, &a,
