div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
CYCLIST UPSET HT A DRUNKEN DRIVER.-MACIEINE
BADLY DAMAGED.

At the Warrington PJlica Court on Tuesday. before /Alderman Shaw Green and Dr Fox, John Cullen, who resides at 15, Eldon-3trcet, was charged with haying been drunk in charge of a spring cart in Winwick-road

at twenty minutes Pig six on Monday evening, also with assaulting P C's Bruen, SAnkey. and Reddington, and further with comnaitting wilful damage to the amount of E 1 to a bicycle, the property of Samuel Pimblett. Samuel Pimblett, a labourer,residing at 275, New Boston, Haydock, said that at about a quarter past six on Monday evening be was going home down Winvrick- road on his bicycle when he saw prisoner driving a horse and cart out of Watkin-street. Prisoner was on the wrong side of the road. Be drove into witness, buckling the front wheel of the bicycle and damaging the machine to the extent of £l. He com- plained to the police, and prisoner was given into custody. He kicked the two police officers and was very rough. P C Bruen said that at the time in question he was in lArinwick-road in company with P C Reddington . . . .

when the last witness complained about the damage to his bicycle. He proceeded along the road and found prisoner, who was drunk. Witness asked him for his name, but defendant refused to give it, and be was taken into custody. Fie commenced to struggle and kicked witness in the back. He also kicked the other police officers. A soldier came up and held defendant down wbile they handcuffed Isim.—The Bench fined defendant 40s and costs for being drunk in charge and assaulting the police, and ordered him to pay the amount of the damage to the bile, or in default to go
to gaol for a month." SEQUEL TO A STRIKE....LABOURER SAVAGELY ASSAULTED
AT GRAPPENHALL.

At the Daresbury Petty Srssinns on Tuesday, before Mr J C Parr and other magistrates, Patrick Collins and Patrick Mulrop, farm labourers, were charged with assaulting an old man, named Thomas Crrhan, a labeurmat Grappenhall the 23rd June. Mr Browne _ _

appeared for the defendants. Complainant stated that hP resided in the shanty at Reddish Hall, Orappenball. On the dry in question he was cooking his dinner in the shanty when the de!eidan Ccllinq told him he had been there too long, and that he had better clear off. He refused to go, and they both kicked him sevPrely, as did a!ro another man, who had since gone away.—By Mr Browne : He (witness) did not pick up an axe and threaten to cut all the men's heads off. He was using the axe to cut some wood. He was not waving the axe round his head. It was not taken from him by one of the defendants to prevent him injuring somPone in the shanty. Matthew Crehan.roa of the last witness gave corroborative evidence. He said his father was kicked insensib!e " by the defendants while he was _

tying on the floor.—By Mr Browne : There waa-a pute about a strike which took place last veal. His father had Riverlthe men no provocation. In answer to the Superintendent of Police (Mr Pearson), witness Said his father threatened to strike one of the defendants with the axe if he did not desist from annoying him.— p.c. Williams, of Grappenhall said he saw the cnmplain- ant on the day in question. His facer-was covered with blood. H- attested the defendants, who denied the cffence. Mr Browne, for the defence, Said that the complainant and his Ron came home from church under the insuence of &irk, and the former commenced to wave the axe about, and threatened to Use it upon the defendants, who came into the shanty at the time, if they did not " clear away." One of the men in the shanty had to knock him down to take the axe from •him, and in falling complainant's head came into CO-- tact with a milking stool, causing an injury. Theyreal wary wag inflicted by a man named Mulroy (a brother Of the defendant Mulroy), who had disappeared since , the assault, hut it was inflicted in self defence owing to the violent conduct of the complalnant.—A, witness who Was in the shanty at the time, said that neither of the defendants struck the complainant, who was brandish- ing an axe about his head, and threatening to "clear •them all out of the house." It was the Mulrey who had gene away who knocked the complainant down. Corn- lainant was unconscious, and was carried into the .neen 11r.—The Bench fined defendants 10i and costs each. , WARRINGTON Dilaw's FIND AND WHAT CA3113 OF jr At the t_ounty Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, before Alderman Fairolough and other magistrates, James Pearce, of Friar's-green,was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Irlam-street at nine o'clock on Tuesday night. —Superintendent Monaghan said that at abut nine o'clock on Tuesday night prisoner went to the Police Station Co report having had some clothes 1 stolen from him. He was drunk and be (the Superinten- dent) advised bin to return when be was sober. From information which was received in the evening about two £5 notes having been lost by a gentleman named Wilittle.,he had his suspicions that prisoner had found them. He accosted prisoner about the matter and be said " Yes, I found them war Singleton's shop, I was as near to a policeman as I am to you. I changed one and bought a suit of clothes and get another man to change the other note." He (the sups int-mdent) found that prisoner had purchased three new suits of clothes, and that the people in the lodging-house had been thinking with the rest of the money. The clothes were taken to the Police Station. He asked the magis- trates to remand orisoner until the following day.—ln ai.swer to a question from the Bench the Superintend- ent said thy man bad 41 or 5,1 of the money left. —The Bench decided to commit the prisoner to gaol for 14 days.

div.head: MINOR UASES.
div.p: MINOR UASES.

Warrington Borough Court. 'ilifiaay.—Before the Mayor (Aldermen Roberts) in the chair, Alderman Monks, Councillors Pierpoint and Smethurst. Mr S Chandley, Air H Thornton, and Mr William Owen. THEFT OF fdaCHlSlTosii—William Henry Boyle, of no address. was charged on remand with stealing a mackintosh from a cloak-roompf the Young Men's Christian:Associaticn Booms a black mackintosh value El, the property of William Samuel Heslop. He pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable recapitulated the facts,stated at the Court a week previously. - The prisoner was seen gadding about the place and on the day the mackintosh was missed,it was found that the prisoner pawned it at Winwick-street for ha:f-a-crown and then left the town. Telephonic messages were sent round the district and the prisoner was apprehended at Prescot where he was handed over to the Borough Police A remand was granted in order that inquires might be made but he (the Chief Constable) had been unable to ascertain laYthints to the man's detriment—The prisoner stated that he was under the influence of drink at the time. If he had been in the same state of mind as he was now it would n,,t have happened. It was the first time he had been arrested.— The Mayor, stated that owing to the fact that there was no pseviona misconduct on the part of the prisoner, and as he And dreadrilfeantgat riser/Mae &week. a conviction would to ..recorded against him, and he would be discharged. A hEcionoo LETTER I MTOSTER,—Thomas Parkinson, described as a labourer of Benk•street was charged with soliciting alms under false pretences.—The Chief Constable stated that in this case he asked for a remand until Thursday

next in order to make some inquiries. About one o'clock I yesterday a complaint was made to the police that the prisoner was going from shop to shop in the town presenting a letter soliciting alms. The letter purported to be written by a works manager at clankey Bridges named John France stating that the mill had been stopped for the past five weeks and that the bearer of the note was in needy circumstances.—The Mayor stated that the prisoner had called at his house and the Mayoress promised to make inquiries with a view of giving I relief. The Chief Constable stated that from inquiries made there was no such parson as France and the prisoner admitted that the whle thing was a forgery and concoction on his part. He (the Chief Constable) was under the impression that this was not the man's first attempt at this kind of thing and he asked for a remand in order to make inquiries. —f he application was granted. A Woßxwas LEAvEs WITHOUT NOTlCE.—Arthur Soden, 10, Sandi:lid-terrace. was summoned at the instance of Messrs S Reynolds and Company, on a charge of leaving his employment without notice and causing damages to the extent of £l.—Mr Taylor represented the complainants and Mr Granger the defendant.—Mr. Taylor explained that the defendant was an offal striker in the employ of the plaintiff company, and had been about five months in their employ- ment. One of the conditions of employment was that it was incumbent upon master and workman to give one week's notice before determining the employment. On the Bth of June the defendant was paid his weekly wage, and did not afterwards come to the tannery. He had Riven no notice of his intention to leave. It was found that he had started work for Mr Maginn, Bridge-street. A difficulty Was experi- enced by the firm in getting another man, and the conse- quence was that overtime had to be paid to some of the other workmen. The delay in dealing with the goods which the defendant ought to have treated had caused injury to the Roods. The defendant was the only offal striker employed. Mr Taylor produced a copy of the rules of working which were affixed in the works and which stipulate that a week's notice was necessary.—Mr John Hartley bore out Mr Taylor's statement, and stated that the damage sustained would be more than EL—For the defence Mr Granger stated that the defendant was engaged to work by the piece. Nothing was said when he was engaged that a week'a notice was necessary. He had not read the rules producedand he submitted that lithe rules were not brought to his notice by the company then they could not set up the statement that he ought to give a week's notice before leav- ing.—The ma dotrates made an order for the payment by the defendant of 2'. _ .

A WORTHLESS HoRSE —Thomas Turner, 56, Battersby-lane was charged at the instance of the Royal Society for the prevention of Cruelty to A,njastals with cruelly illtreating a horse by working It in an meg, state.—lnartector Print stated that the horse was lame and was suffering from an incurable disease. It w•s unfit for any work.—Superinten- dent Monaghan and Inspector Wilson gave Corroborative evidence and on the defendant undertaking not to work it again,he was tined the costs only. A WINDOW BREAKER.—Mary Dodd, 11, Stephen street was charged with wilfully breaking the windows of Frank Lancaster Martin—The defendant admitted having smashed four windows but contended that she was provoked to it by the complainant's son striking her with an axe—She was ordered to put the windows in and p y 7s. costs. A RESERVIST AND lin WlFE—William Farrington, a reservist of the South Lancashire Regiment now on furlough and residing at 11, Plfillip-street,was charged with persistent cruelty to his wire, Catherine Farrington, thereby causing her to leave him.—The complainant Stated that her husband had thrashed her several times and she left him. He had not given her anything since she left him.—ln cross-examination witness admitted that she had "five drinks" on the night on which she fell out with blm.—The defendant said he was a reservist on furlough and had been allowed to return to his work. He took part in the engagements which led to the relief of Ladysmith when he was invalided home. He had got work and rffered to take her back but she would not live with him—The complainant said "it was a good job to get abut of you "—The magistrates then dismissed the case and Mr Taylor was asked to see if he csuld induce the parties to live together. WIFE DESERTION.—Patrick Walsh, 29, New-road, was charged with deserting his wife Eleanor Walsh.—Mr Steel appeared for the complainant and stated that the defendant was a filecutter and had been married to the complainant 30 years. They had had 17 children, and seven were now living. Lately the defendflit had been constantly drunk and after abusing his wife he left her.—The defendant said be had, given way to drink owing to his wife's drunken habits. He had asked her to abstain from drink and he had promised to do the same.—The magistrates ordered the defendant to coatribute lOs a week towards his wife's maintenance.
SATURDAY. —Before Mr Et_ T Fairelough. (In the. chair),
Alderman Heaton and Councillor John Roberta.

THE -SUSPICIOUS CONDUCT OF A. WOMAN—Mary Ellen Poden was charged on remand with being found in posses- sion of a pair of boots on Wednesday morning without being able to give a satisfactory account of how she obtained them The Chief Constable i:.formed the Bench that the prisoner was found wandering about in the small hours of Wednes- day morning by Police-constable Turner She was far gone In liquor, and had a pair of new boots which she could not account for at all. She made several conflicting statements among others that Couneillor Bacon of Warrington, had Riven tbem to her but of course that Councillor was a myth. No owner had been found for the boots, and he would have to ssk that the prisons be discharged. Mr Taylor, pollee court missionary,would bee that she returned home to Urms- ton.—The prisoner was accordingly discharged. MONDAY—Before Mr Hayward (in the chair) Alderman
Heaton, Councillor S'rnethursst rind Mr Tho'rnton.

PRIDGET OURLMY IN THOUS Lk AG &IN.—Bridget Curley, a widow, who now made her 18th appearance, was charged with sleeping at the rear of a house in Wilson Patten-street, on the previous night without any means of subsistenee.— PC Howard stated the facts.—Alderman Heaton asked the old woman why she did not go to the Workhouse, and she replied that she would do anything rather than go there. It was stated that she had been sent there several times. but that she would not remain.—The Bench committed her to goal for 14 days. CRUELTY TO HOR,E9.—Themas Bailey. of Poster-street. was summoned for having on the 15th June ill-treated a horse by working it while in an unfit state.—lnspector Print, of the 8.5.P.C.A., detailed the facts cf the case. —Defendant told the Bench that he was willing to have the horse destroyed, and the case was adjourned for a week to enable him to carry out his promise. He was also ordered to pay the costs.—David 61cCririe. of Winwlck-road, was charged with a similar offence, and was fined 6s.—lnspector Print also proved this case. A SATURDAY NIGHT SCENE LN THE MARIKET —Patrick Police, 13, Dutton-street, fish hawker. John Longshaw. Lythgoes-lane, greengrocer, and William Lowe. Brwood- street, fish-hawker,were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in the Market-place on the 15th June. —John Clough said the offence took place at 11.45. and Willism Whittaker, who has a stall in the market, said that several rounds were fought by the men. One of them took off his shirt. —P.C, Clough said he was called to the distur- bance, and th men admitted that they had been fighting in self-deferce.—The Chief Constable : There was a great deal of the noble art of self-defence (Laught.r.)—P.C. Clough : Yes. Mr.—The defendants practically admitted the offence, and were bound ova- to keep the peace for six months. in their own surety of £5 each, and ordered to pay the costs of the case.

--- TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Shaw Green (la the chair) and Dr. Fox. D,MESTIC TROUBLES.—SamueI Sutcliffe. greengrocer, 21. Bowes-street, was charged on 5.-warrant with assaulting and , beating his wife. Martha Sutcliffe. on Saturday afternoon.— ' Mrs Sutcliffe said that at half past five on Saturday afternoon she went out to look for prisoner and found him in a beer- house. He went out the back way and ran through Silver- I street. She afterwards saw him at his brother's house. He butted' her in the face with his head and dragged her into the yard by her hair. He also kicked her on the nose and head and left her there "bleeding like a dog."—The Chief Constable said that when complainant applied for the warrant the told the Beach that prisoner broke her nose by kicking her —Pt isoner said his wife was drunk, and he pushed her and she ie.!. 55., also stated that he lied been illtreated by his wife.—Dr. Fox, was of the opinion that it was " aix of one , half a dozen of the oti.er." The magistrates discharged the prisoner with a caution, and it was understood that Mr. Taylor, the Police Court Missionary, would give the case his attention. ALLEGED THEFT OF Lawrenson, Was charged with steeling from a lodging house, 11, Stanley- street. on Saturday, a pair of clogs,valued at 25.. the property of John Delaney.—The Chief Constable said prosecutor was a labourer and lodged at this house in Stanley street. Pris- oner also lodged there. On Saturday afternoon prosecutor left his clogs near a sofa on which the prisoner was lying. He missed the clogs later, but did not give any information to the police until Monday. Prisoner was then in other lodg- ings and the clogs were found under his bed.—Delaney gave evidence in support of the above statement, and P.C. Clough deposed to arresting defendant. Prisoner said he did not know how he came in possession of the clogs, and the prose- cutor said he might have put them on by mlstake.—The Chairman said that after what prosecutor said.they were ound to discharge defendant. A VAGRANT.—Mary Jane Mooney, of no settled ablde, was charged with sleeping out in an unoccupied house in Percival's-fold on Tuesday morning, without having any visible means of subsistence.—P.U. Wyse proved the case, aud prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days.

div.head: Daresbury Petty Sessions.
div.p: Daresbury Petty Sessions.
itiESDAY.—Before Mr C Parr tin the chair), Mr H Meld
and Mr F Monks.

ILLEGAL REMOVAL -0-1-9—ViLN-ET-Liiiii;LY TREATED BY THE BOARD or Aoßrcrramir.--Thomas Hnsworth was summoned for having on the 31st May, at Stockton Heath, acted in con- travention of the Swine Fever Order, 1894, by allowing a pig to be moved from an infected place. Sergeant Bourne proved the case, and stated that a pig had been slaughtered and taken to a Warrington shop for sale. He had seen the defendant, who told him he bad been badly treated by the Board of Agriculture, and that it was no encouragement to report cases of swine fever Defendant now said he had misnaderstood what the sergeant had said to him or he would not have slaughtered a fat pig for which he had been paid £7. He reported aces° of swine fever seven weeks ago Oue pig was killed, and since that • time out of the 40 animals he had not one had' gone." He (defendant) was in a peculiar position. Formerly coxpensation was ',aid to a farmer. but now none was given and his hands were tied. A fine of Ei and Cost 3 was inflicted.—John Walley was Charged with a breach of the Diseases Animals' Act, 1894, by makings false declaration in regard to the removal of 10 pigs at Anlrobus on the sth June. Mr W Bancroft, of Northwich defended. Evi.lence was given by the police to alsoW that I the declaration wrongly stated that the pigs (which had come from Huntingdonshire) had been on defendant's premises 28 days, whereas they had been tt.ere only one day. For the defence Mr Bancroft said it was not a wilfully false declaration, although it might have been an unlawful declaration, the original delaration having been delayed by the railway company. There had been no guilty knowledge on his p rt, and. therefore no criminal offence had been committed. The defendant was only in a small woy of business, end had had only four or live consignments of animals. The Chairman said the Bench Were satisfied that an offence had been committed, although under misapprehension, and a fine of Et and costs would be imposed. S.ringent instructions had been received that these cases were to be severely dealt with. div.head: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions.

MONDAY.—Before Mr AR Norman and Mr Samuel Taylor. A FURTHER AIVoURNMENT.—The adjourned hearing of the alleged desertion by Thomas Wood of his wife Kate Rthel Wood,resulted in a further adjournment to the 15th of July. —The facts of the case show the parties to have been married about 2i years. After marriage they took up their abode with the wife's mother at 33, Portland-street, Runcorn. De- fendant was described as being difficult to get out of bed " in the morning, and on this point he and the mother-in-law often " fell out." He left the house, which was in his name, and had gone to Lostock Graham, about the 12th of May,since which time he had only sent his wife 3s. Ile was desirous of having his wife to,live with him at Lostoak, but he would not live with the mother-in.law.—The Bench, after long consideration, adjourned the case as stated. in the hope that the parties would come to some understanding. There was no evidence to show that the hus- band had been unkind or cruel, or that be had deserted his wife. Therefore, they advised her to go with her husband for the three weeks,:foand a,little home, and settle tkeir difficulties. OTHER CASES.—Bobert Lloyd, Hughes' Court, and William Percival, 10 Alcock-street, had to pay 4s 6d costs because their chimneys had been on fire.—Jam Fahy, labourer, Granville-street, was fined 5s for being drunk and disorderly In Church-street ; and John Inglesfield, an old Offender (last of St. Helens), was fined 5s and Is 6d costs or seven days, for being drunk and fighting in Stone-street.

AMERICANS AND THE SALT TRADE.

Intention to Absorb the Salt Union. NEW YORK, TUESDAY. Despite press denials received from England, says the New York Correspondent of the "Manchester Gnar- -1 dian " the Salt Company officials here declared to-day lln the most positive manner their intention to absorb the English Salt Union. They affirmed that the new International Trust in process of formation would be formed on the pattern and financed in the same way as I the Steel Trust—that is, an international concern will be formed to take over the shares of the constituent companies in return for its own securities. In cases where such an exchange is possible cash value will be offered. Outlining the plans of the new Company, one official said to me to-day : " Great Britain is a hundred years behind the times in the salt industry. Over there they seem content to pursue old methods, disregarding the Improvements that have given the imerican plants such 1 a headway. As a matter of fact, the international I concern, with American ' push and up-to-date machinery, could clear from Idols. to &lois. on every 1 ton of salt marketed. That is a neat profit, and indi- cates tbe possibilities of an undertaking which will do I much for the salt industry throughout the world." NEW YORK, TUESDAY. It is reported that the International Salt Trust is practically completed, with a capital of about fifty million dollars. The trust includes the National Salt Company (United States),the Salt Union (England),and the Canadian Salt Company. It will be known as the International Salt Company, and will be controlled by the Rockefellers and se- 'rat of their associates.

FAREWELL TO THE REV. J. T. SCHOFIELD. • Interesting Presentations on Thursday Evening Striking evidence of the esteem in which the Rev ' J T Schofield has been held by the members of the congregation during his five years' ministry at Golborne-street Baptist Church, was afforded on Thursday last week,when a meeting was held in the chapel for the purpose of bidding him farewell on his leaving the town,and presenting him with some tangible recognition of his services. As has previously been announced in the "Examiner," Mr Schofield has accepted a call to North-street Baptist Church, Leeds. He came to Warrington nearly five years ago from Northamptonshire, to take up the pastorate of Golborne-street Church. During his ministry there,the rev gentleman has instituted the monthly evangelistic service, and taken charge of the Sunday school girls' Bible class, in addition to the pastorate work of the church. When it be- came known that he was about to sever his connec- tion with the church much regret was expreseed and the deacons at once commenced to make ar- rangements for presenting him with some mark of the esteem which is entertained for him. The con- gregation liberally responded to the request for con- tributions, ana on Thursday evening Mr Schofield was the recipient of a purse containing £2O in gold, and a handsome framed photograph ot himself and the deacons of the church. Prior to the public meet- ing, a social gathering took place in the schoolroom and refreshments were served. The meeting in the Chapel was presided over by Mr B Few, and amongst others present were the Revs J S liughes, J F Matthews, Theodore Bishop, C Finch, E T Reed and Messrs Balinford, Heywood, and H Buckby. The Rev John Yonge was unable to he present and sent a letter of apology, in which he said that had he been present he should have given very earnest expression of his regard and esteem for Mr Schofield. Eor the sake of Golborne-street Chapel and the Warrington Free churches generally, he very much regretted that Mr Schofield was leaving the town. He had been held in great re•pect by them all, and his brother ministers, while sorry to lose him, wished him heartily, a very happy career in the church and town to which he was removing. The Grumman. in the course of a brief opening speech, said that as members of the church they must sympathise with one another in the loss they were about to sustain in the removal of their pastor,but on the other hand they rejoiced that Mr Schofield was going forth to another sphere of labour under such happy circum- stances. They who had worked in what might be termed the inner circle of the church knew what their pastor bad been: They had sometimes differed with him, but they had always differed to agree. (Hear,hear.) Mr Schofield had made rules and regulations which he (Mr Few) thought had been for the betterment of the church. They were pleased that Mr Schofield was going up the ladder. (Hear, hear.) He had been a backbone Christian, and he (the chair- man) hoped he would be successful in the work which he bad undertaken in Leeds. (Applause.) Mr Few proceeded to speak of the good work which bad been done by Mrs Schofield, and said he did not think they could hate had a pleasanter minister's wife. In con- clusion he said the efforts of Mr and Mrs Schofield had not been in vain. They had sown seed which would in time bring forth fruit. Mr Schofield bad not only preached sermons but had lived sermons, and this had been for the good of the church. (Applause.) Mr BALDIFORD then made the presentation, and in doing so, said his duty was a pleasant but at the same time painful one. Mr Schofield came among them five years ago and when he had been in Warrington three years he received a hearty and unanimous invitation to another church—a church which he (the speaker) knew had special attractions for him. He was very much tempted to go but thinking it to be the will of God he declined the offer. He had now been with them five years and was about to leave them. He (the speaker) bad been asked bow it was that when they were so united in the church and had such hopeful prospects before them, that Mr Schofield was leavieg,and be could only answer that Mr Schofield believed it to be the will of God that he should go. All through his ministry that bad been his guiding principle. The one bright spot in that event was that Mr Schofield was leaving under such happy conditions. He was going away with the hearty g eed wistaes of the whole of the members of the church ar.d congregation and with a standing invitation to return as soon as the people at Leeds were tired of him or be was tired of them. (Laughter.) He was sure Mr Schofield would have a happy and successful career in his new sphere of labour. As to the success of bis work in Warrington it was too early yet to estimate that. He had been in a great measure en- gaged in pulling down and also in foundation work and the longer he had remained among them the more they had been able to appreciate his work and character. They who knew the church knew that real successful work had been done. The standard which Mr Schofield had set up had been a high moral and spirtual tone, and though this had not tended to numerical success, at the same time, it had been a proof of his sincerity and earnestness that he had been willing to suffer himself in consequence. Finan- cially the church Wag never in a better position (Applause.) Last year they raised more than they bad ever done previously, and during the first half of the present year the ordinary weekly offerings were twenty per cent, better than they were in the first six months of last year. He questioned whether there was another church in Warrington with such a record for this year. They were not unmindful of the part Mrs Schofield bad taken in the work of the Church. What they owed to her very few had any idea. She had been an ideal minister's wife, blessed with a special measure of womanly tact and kindness. Mr Balmford then banded the gifts to Mr. Schofield amid loud applause. The Rev THEODORE BISHOP, who had attended for the purpose of making a presentation to Mr Schofield on behalf of the Free Church Ministers' Fraternal,of which Mr Schofield has been secretary, then made a few remarks. He said be had been in that town nearly two years and had known Mr Schofield and bad learnt to love him. They would find he was a good fellow. (Hear, hear.) When he (Mr Bishop) was admitted to the Fraternal,Mr Schofield was secretary, and he (Mr Bishop) bad experienced many kindnesses from Wm. He con- gratulated him upon the handsome tokens of esteem which belied just received from the congregation. The members of the Fraternal had subscribed together to make him a present, and he (Mr Bishop) had pleasure in handing him a fountain pen, a stylographic pen and pocket book. (Applause). The Rev ,J S HUGHES said he had had the honour of knowine Mr. Schofield longer than any other minister in the district. He came to him (Mr. Hughes) on the occasion of his first visit to Warrington, and he (Mr Hughes) gave him such a character of the congregation at Golborne-street, as prob- ably determined him to settle among them. From the commencement he had entertained a very high opinion of Mr Schofield as a man,as a brother minister, and as a pastor. When he heard that there was a prospect of him taking his departure he thought ittwas a very serious step,because he believed Mr Scho- field was doing a very necessary and important work, and would not for some years reap the fruits of his labours and toil. That church was not an easy church to undertake the pastorate of. He had generally found that in towns where the Congregationalists were strong, the Baptists were proportionately weak,and that might account in some measure for the difficulty in connection with that church. He (Mr Hughes) thought that as a church they were doing well, and he hoped that when Mr Schofield had taken his departure they would cling well together and face the difficulties, so that by and by there would be a strong and influential church there. He had been an admirer of Mr Schofield's sturdy inde- pendence, and his determination to carry out his con- victions and wished him every success in the future. (Applause,) The Rev C Freer( also spoke in eulogistic terms of the work accomplished by Mr Schofield. The Rev J F MATTHER3 made a short speech and trueted that Mr Schofield would make an impression upon the civic and religious life of the place to which he was going, and rise to some eminence in the church. No people would be more pleased to hear of his success than the congregation of Golborne-street. Mr Schofield had been a hardworking, faithful, loving, devoted and conscientious pastor. (Applause.) The Rev E T REED 3180 addressed the gathering, In responding, Mr SCHOFIELD said the photograph with which they had presented him would of times recall the very happy times be had spent with the deacons of the Church. Ministers owed a great deal to the deacons, for as a rule they were their very best friends, and certainly upon the diaconate depended to a great extent the harmony and welfare of the Church. He believed the deacons of that Church were the true representatives of the church and the cream of the church and it was with pleasure that he accepted the photograph. Mr Schofield mentioned the fact that four of the deacons were on the diaconate when he came to the church and they had occupied the position ever since. With regard to the purse of gold he was pleasantly surprised with the amount of the present. Knowing the many calls upon their liberality he felt that the amount they had subscribed was a strong ex- pression of their appreciation of his services, and of good wishes concerning his future career. In returning thanks for the gifts from the Fraternal, he said he had always been on very happy terms of good fellowship with his ministerial brethren and it bad been a privilege for him to serve as Secretary c the Fratenal. Continuing he said be should al wa; look back upon Warrington with affection. He ehoul remember it as the place of their first home and as ti place where he spent nearly five years of a very hap; ministry. He-believed there was in that church tht making of a strong Baptist Church. He had experienced

A LOCAL SCHOOLTVIASTER FINE D
Alleged Severe Thrashing of Scholars
at Croft.

Case of considerable interest to eche- I teacerrs were heard at the Warrington County Petty Sessions last week, before Colonel Ridgway (presiding) awl Mr F A Frost.—Caroline Ashley,a resident in Croft, was charged with having assaulted James Cawthorne, head master of Croft Board Schools on the 4th June. Mr Caw.horee was counter-summoned for having assaulted Caroline Elizabeth Ashley, daughter of the first defendant, on the same date.—Mr Jenkins appeared for the t,ead- master, and Mr Knowles for Mrs Ashley. Both parties pleaded not guilty and the cases were taken conjointly. Mr Jenkins said Mrs Aihley was the mother of four children, two boys and two girls who attended the Croft Board Schools where his client was the headmaster. On the date in quiestion Caroline Elizabeth Ashley,daughter of the defendant, went to school in the morning about SO minutes late. The headmaster enquired from her the reason of her lateness,and she said she had beenaent by her mother to take her brother's baggiu." The headmaster objected to this as not being a sufficient excuse and gave the girl two slight taps on the arm with a cane and sent her to her place. He did not do this as a punishment but only just tapped her and told her not to be late again. Lie then found that she had not got her slate and other accessories to a child's education and he sent her into the vestibule to get them. She left the room, and having closed the door after her ran off altogether. About a 0 minutes later Mr Cawthorne saw the girl Ashley's mother come into the yard, evidently in a very angry state. Desirous of avoiding any bother likely to ensue, Mr Cawthorne went to the door for the purpose of intercepting the defendant and tendering any ex- planation which she desired. She, however, forced herself Past him into the schools, attempting to strike Mr Cawthorne, who, however, avoided the blows. Her conduet was shocking, and she used very bad language. They flid not ask for a substantial fine to be inflicted but took the proceedings in order to prevent a re- currence of the scene of an angry mother forcing her way into the schools and interrupting the children's studies.

Mr Cawthorne said that whsn the defendant got past him into the schools she commenced to shout and create a disturbance, and used most abusive language to him before all the children. The school was rown into confusion for twenty minutes. By Mr Knowles: Parents had never complained to him about having thrashed children in a merciless and brutal manner:

_ By Mr Jenkins : He always infLicted punishment humanely and judiciously whenever necessary Cross-examined : He did not attempt in any way to g strike Mrs Ashley. Mrs Ashley did not touch him, but tried her best to do so. He only ave the little girl two slight taps on the arm. Herbert Priestner and John Thomas Qaane cor- robarated. For the defence Mr Knowles contended that no assault had been committed, as on the scnoolmaster's own admission Mrs Ashley had never struck him. The fact of her using bad language, or even threats and having attempted to strike him did not constitute an assault. As regarded the case against Mr Cawthorne he contended that the schoolmaster had outstepped the bounds of the position in which every schoolmaster was necessarily placed. His position should simply be one in loco parentis. Lie would call evidence to prove that instead of giving her two slight taps on the arm, Mr Cawthorne thrashed the girl severely, Caroline Elizabeth Ashley, aged 11 years, said she attende I Croft Board School. When she gave her excuse for being late on the 4th June, the master gave her about 20 severe blows with a cane on the arm and back. Phe ran off home crying to her mother' who returned to school with her. Her mother did not hit Mr Cawthorne, but Mr Cawthorne raised his fist to her mother. Joseph Daintith, a scholar at the schools, said he saw the schoolmaster hit the little girl about 20 times. Mrs Ashley said she had often complained about the way in which her children were treated at the schools. On the 4th June her little girl came home crying very bitterly and complained that the head master had been thrashing her. She examined her daughter and found several black marks on her back and one on her arm. , She went to the schools for the purpose of taking her other children away. She did not strike or attempt to strike the head master, but she did call him names by way of retaliation as be called her a bad, uncivilised woman. Mrs uixen, neighbour of Mrs Ashley, corroborated, and said that the head master tried to strike Mrs. Ashley. Mr. Knowles held that the girl's lateness was not sufficient justification for the infliction of such a severe thrashing as his witnesses had proved was inflicted. If the child went late repeatedly the master had his remedy. He could refuse to record a mark in the regis- ter for attendance, and then prosecute the parents for , the non-attendancs of their children. Both oases were dismissed.

James Cawthorn was then further charged with having assaulted Fred Ashley on the 2llth April. Mr 'Jenkins on behalf of his client, pleaded not guilty. ...Mr Knowles said that on Friday, the Seth April, the children had:been dismissed from school at 3 30 o'clock. Adjoining the school was a disused field which was used as the sch3ol playground and as was usual in the after- noon the children were let out for 10 minutes play-time during which period they with the Master's sanction set fire to the dead grass. After leaving school the boys ttending the school went home, had their tea. and re- turned to again burn the crass. Cawthorne's little boy was out with the other lads and be gave the boy 'Ashley a push which sent him into some of the blazing grass. Ashley objected to this and he and Cawthorne's boy commenced to fight. Mrs Cawthorne, seeing this, sent her servant girl out to smack the lads who were hitting , her little boy. The girl, in accordance with instructions, went out and began to belabour Ashley and another lad named Daintitb. Daintith retaliated, and instead of the servatit smacking him Daintith smacked her. The servant went back into the I house, and the schoolmaster went into the field. 'He asked the lad Daintith to catch Ashley. Daintith made a pretence of catching Ashley, but the two subse- quently left the field, the master having-retired into the schools. The two boys were later in the day proceeding alone the walk past the school when Mr Cawthorn° jumped over the wall, and seizing them, took them into school and thrashed them. This oocurred long after school hours; there the schoolmaster became as an ordinary individual and as such infl,cted gross Cruelty on these two boys. Mr. Knowles went on 'to say that if the boys had complained to the N B.P.C.C. Inspector the schoolmaster would have made himself liable to a very much more severe penalty -than was now the case. Mr Jenkins : Lam loath to interfere, but that con- jecture cannot be accepted. Contiauing, Mr Knowles said as it wes defendant had made himself liable to a line of £5 or to two months' imprisonment with hard labour without the option of a fine. Fie asked for a substantial penalty in that case. The children must be protected and he knew of many cases similar to that which had been hushed up. Joseph D iintith corroborated Mr Knowles' statement and said that when the master took them into the school to thrash them he locked the door. Witness was not thrashed very much, but Ashley was thraf h0(1 very badly. Mx Cawthorn° held Ashley's i-,ands while he hit him with the cane about the legs. Ashler, fell down, but Mr Cawthorne still continued to punish hiin,hitting him about the back. So severe was the punishment that Mr Cawthorne's wife even earns and asked him to s,op hitting :hem. Mrs ishloy came after they had been in the room about 20 minutes and commenced kicking at the door. Mr Cawthorne let them out of another door. Ele (witness) afterwards saw Ashley's legs which were covered with black marks as a result of the blows.

div.head: NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
div.p: NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor. Matters intended for publicadon must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible not later than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary cireumstar cos under- take to return the manuscripts which are not used.

div.head: Corporation Contracts.
div.p: Corporation Contracts.

Sir,—There is one paragraph, and one only, in Mr I James Dodds' epistle of last week, which seems to have any bearing on my previous letter. That parsgraph is the first, in which he alludes to my description of his conduct as " unchristian " and seems disinclined to discuss the matter. Perhaps your correspondent is wise in this respect. Life is, certainly, much too short to fully discuss and settle definitely the question of the " christianity "of Mr. James Dodds' conduct. I wonder how your readers like him in the role of self-constituted judge of public men whose services to the town are as valuable and great as those of Mr Dodds are infinitesimal. Yours !so, MAXIM.

Sir.—l feel it due to you (and to myself) that I should notice your remarks upon my last letter. Your comments are fairly summariaed in your assertion that 1 "harp upon the same string and endeavour to twist what is legally right into something which Is morally wrong, and at the same time to cast odium upon one of our most respected townsmen." You must have known very well, with my letter before you, that my position in regard to this question was that that which was— and is still—strictly legal is now universally held to bQ wrong and immoral. And as to the casting of odium upon one of our most respected towns men—the Mayor to wit,—you must be well aware that it was the Mayor himself who first condemned what—in my letter—l condemned, for in November last—after the enforced retirement of the Lord Mayor- elect of Manchester and others—the Mayor had a document prepared by his solicitor, assigning his own and family's shares of the Warrington Slate Company's profits from Corporation contracts to others. Why did the Mayor do this if not because he was satisfied that though it was legal it was wrong and immoral to receive such profits ? Of course my contentions go further, and I hold aping.; all corners that the only satisfactory plan is for the Mayor either to resign his seat, or for hi s company to cease all direct or indirect trading witb the Corpora- tion,—l am Rze. JAMES DODDg. June 21st.

Our main contention was that Mr Dodds advanced nothing new. and that if he was dissatisfied with the law for legalising something which appears to him Im- moral, he should tilt at the law and not at individuals. Such appears to us the only fair, sensible, and practical course, and we still adhere to our contention.—Editor, " Examiner."'

Sir,—lt is regrettable that the press of the town should condescend to print a tale of unsubstantiated scandal and gossip such as is contained in Mr James Dodds' letter printed last Saturday. Mr Dodds' letter is particularly objectionable in that his language is so carefully guarded as to leave no foundation for an action for libel. I suggest that if Mr Dodds has the courage of his opinions, instead of enveloping his scan- dalous imputations in so much beautiful language about morality, he shall write and publish a few lines to the effect that Mr Alderman So-and-So or Mr Cauncillor Tomnoddy is robbing or cheating the ratepayers by the means he suggests. Then perhaps we shall have the decision of a Court of Law on the question, and either 1 tha members of the Cauncq implicated or Mr Dodds will be exposed. I believe Mr Dodds is a pillar of his particular sect of religion. Perhapa he will remember a text in one of the gospels which says "Let him that is without sin cast the first stone " or words to that effect. Just one further remark. The cases to which Mr Dodds refers at Manchester and Balton are in no wise analagous to the cases of Alderman Roberts or Alderman Franconab. They were cases of individuals or members of private firms, not limited companies trading with the Corporations of which the persons concerned respec- tively were members. I am not in the Council nor interested in any way in Corporation business. lam a mere ratepayer -whose rates are being increased inter alia by the erratic con- duct of Dodds, Gough, Cliffe and Co, and lam utterly sick of bearing these scandals talked about which Ido not believe to exist. Yours &a., LUX FIAT. 21st June, 1901.

Sir,—I have received the following letter from Mr W B J Jenkins, Solicitor, who was for some years a member of the Town Council, and, as it has an import- ant bearing upon the above question, I shall be obliged if you will publish it in your next issue.—Thanking you in anticiPat, Yours faithfully, II ROBERTS, Mayer. --- Carlton Cottage, Stockton Ileatb, June 22ad, 1901. Dear Mr Mayor,—May I offer you a word of sympathy at this time when it seems to me an unfair method of attack is being made on your position as a citisen. For years it has been known that the Company in which you and your family are largely interested was doing business with the Corporation. If this fact made you unworthy to occupy the highest offiee the town can confer upon a man, why did not those who disapprove of yoar public life make a strenuous effort-to prevent your attaining that position ? Such a line of action would at least have been within the rules of fair play. I have always thought that, when a man has been elected to the Mayoral office, all differences, political, religious, or otherwise should be sunk in a generous and loyal de- sire to support the chief citizen that his office may be upheld with dignity and calmness, and that he should be strengthened in his work by the feeling that he has the sympathy of " all sorts and conditions of men." When I was a member of the Finance Committee of the Corporation, an informal but none the less searching investigation was made as to your position in the Council and especially in relation to the fact that the Warrington Slate Company was doing business with thetCorporation. Without going closely into detail I would say that your position and that of the Company were found to be unimpeachable and to that fact I have pleasure in testifying. • My reason for writing you is that in my opinion, just now, you!are being hit below the belt and for the reasons which I have before mentioned being treated in an ungenerous manner. —1 remain yours faithfully, W' JENKINS.
J The Worshipful The Mayor, Henry Roberts, Egg., J P, Warrington.

March out of Volunteers. About 600 members of the local Volunteers corps paraded at the Drill Hail, on Saturday afternoon to take part in a march out to Parlgate. The men fell in at four o'clock at the Drill Hall,the Mounted Infantry Company assembling at the Riding School, in Parker-street, and the cycling corps out- side the Drill Hall. The battalion marched out at 4.30, being preceded by an advance company under the command ef Major Buckton. The other officers on parade were Captains J Dutton Fairclough and G.R. Croafield, Lieutenant Roberts, and Second- Lieutenants Ridgway and Avery. They marched to Padßate, and on arrival there proceeded to a couple of helds,kindly lent by Mr William Bennett Where they went through several interesting, raancouvTes ovinc.; to the state of the weather rain descehnz,heavily, tl'E Volunteers returned home earlier than had been arranged, namely at about seven o'clock.

div.head: LATEST NEWS. Alleged Attempt to Wreck a
div.p: LATEST NEWS. Alleged Attempt to Wreck a
_ Scotch Express. Arrest of a Cheshire Signalman.

The discovery of an alleged attempt at train wrecking was made at 11.30 on Wednesday night on the London and North• Western Railway, near Minshull Vernon Station, Cheshire. Detective- Inspector Morgan, Crewe, proceeding on a light engine, found a large piece of wood wedged between the points on the up line and two sleepers placed side; by side across the down line. The Scotch express from Liverpool was due in ten minutes. It was a dark night, and the train would have been wrecked but for the prompt removal of the obstruction. At Middlewich Police Court, yesterday morn- ing, Joseph Minshull, North-Western signalman, living at Sydney, near Crewe, was charged with attempted train wrecking. The evidence showed that the prisoner was last night on duty in a signal box near the station, and the wood discovered in the points fitted a piece found in a store beneath his box. No other person was on duty near the station. Detectives Perkins and Morgan.were dis- satisfied with Minshull's answers and he was arrested, tie was remanded to Thursday next, bail refused.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. CAPE COLONY. Determined Attack on Richmond.
Enemy Forced to Retire.

A Reuter telegram says the Boers, wider Com- mandants Malan and Smit, attacked Richmond (Cape Colony) on Wednesday morning. The attack lasted till dusk, when the enemy retired, probably hearing of the approach of Captain Lund's column.

div.head: HONOURING RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS. A Magnificent Spectacle at the Drill Hall.
div.p: HONOURING RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS. A Magnificent Spectacle at the Drill Hall.

The Drill Hall, Runcorn,was, on Wednesday evening, thronged to its utmost capacity, the occasion heing the presentation of inscribed solid silver lever watches to the returned Volunteers and Yeomanry, who have served with the colours in the recent war in South Africa. All shades of Runcorn Society were present,from the Mayor to the newsboy ; parson to choir-boy ; each distinc- tive linkwas strikingly represented ; for all had' contributed to the occasion and allyrere entitled to par tici pate therein. The arrangements of the proceedings in themselves afforded an object lesson. Die Runcorn Orchestral Society (under Mr Horace Hindley), and the following vocalists Miss Simkin, Miss P Humphreys, Mr E Johnson, Mr E Worrell, with Miss Barbara Johnson as accompanist delighted the audience with capital musi- cal items. The former was responsible for " Light Cavalry," "Two Brass Men" " Brisnuits " and the "German Patrol ;" Miss Simkins for "Angus McDon- ald ; " Miss Humphreys for "Enchantress," 'Rory Darbut," and " Rule Britannia." Both ladies were in capital voice and were highly commended for their exceedinglypelightful contributions. Mc Edgar John- son gave with great success "Stand by the Old Flag of England," and Mr E. Worrell, the ever popular tenor, was good in "The Bay of Biscay. After the musicians had played their part, the plat form was occupied by Mrs R H Posnett (who had kindly undertaken to make the presentation and to un- veil the " roll of honour "), Meesrs R El Posnett (chair- man U.D.C), W Handley (vice-chairman), S Taylor, J.P., E unison, J.P., C.C., S Walton, J Wilson, E Marshall, J Wilding, M ijor Harrison, Captain George F Ashton, Captain Timmins, Mrs Imison, Miss Garnett, Mr Garnett, Ice. Mr S Taylor, upon whom fell the honour of intro- ducing Mrs Posnett, said be felt there was little need for that portion of the ceremony, Mrs Posnett had not been in the town many years, but, in the short time spent amongst them, had endeared herself to all by the practical sympathy she extended to all the goo cl work carried on. (Applause.) They delighted to seeper pre- sent to carry out the very pleasurable duty of making the presentations and unveiling the "roll of honour " (bear hear and applause)—that magnificent piece of work on the wall—and presenting it to their own volunteers. (Applause.) How much the services of those volunteers were appreciated was exemplified by the large gathering of people present. It was no little thing for those young men to have volunteered—to have left their comfortable homes, with their luxuries and enjoyments, to go out and fight for their Ring and country. (Applause.) They had also hardships to en- dure out there, often having to go without food and water, as well as lose their rest day and night. Those were things, that unless they thought seriously about them, they could not appreciate. (Cheers.) Having spoken of the pleasure with which the country had been filled at the nobte response of the Volunteers and Yeo- manry, the speaker also referred to the grand reception they were now receiving upon their return. (Applause) He had great pleasure in calling upon Mrs Posaett to present the watches. (Applause.) The watches, beautifully engraved solid silver English levers, were supplied by Mr 'l' S Carr, Regent-street, and prior to them being handed over. Captain Ashton read aloud the inscription on one, which was as follows :—" Presented to Sergeant Frederick John Jeacock, la Company, E.C., Volunteer Battalion, Cheshire Regiment, by the inhabitants of Runcorn on his return from active service with the Cheshire Volunteer Company, in the Boer war, South Africa 1399-1901." Captain Ashton added the inscriptions were of a similar character on the others; the name only being different. The inscription on the watch presented to Trooper Bankes, styled him as such, and as having served with " the 21st Company Cheshire Imperial Yeomanry." Mrs Posnett then very gracefully asked each of the " Warriors "to accept the watches. They came up in the following order,the cavalry being in the rear :—Ser- geant F J Jeacock, Lance-Corporal F J Speakman, Trooper Horatio Stanley Victor BankeS,Corperal F Mack and Corporal F Platt. E soh man received quite an ovation, and having shaken hands with Mr and Mrs Posnett took his seat at the back of the platform.

Captain Timmins described his duty as an honour and pleasure. It was to thank the piahlic of Runcorn and district for the very generous manner in which they had supported the function. Having _done so with characteristic heartiness, Captain TirnminS also ten. dared the thanks of all to Mrs Posnett for 80 gracefully and willingly accepting her duties of the night and per- forming them in a gracious manner. (Applause ) Mr E Liaison, C.C., who was called upon to respond on behalf of the townspeople,appreciated the difficulties of replying on other people's behalf. Yet, he felt safe in saying it had been a real pleasure to them to subscribe the sum necessary to make that presenta- tion, and a great privilege to take part in that meetifig. which had been such an undoubted success. (Applause.) He paid a high tribute to the workingmen of the town for their share in the work, and did not forget the efforts they had put forward in connection with the other war funds. (Applause.) The heartiness with which the gifts were given he was Bare would add to the pleasure of .those who received them. (Applause.) After all, he Still considered they were debtors to the Volunteers, and it would have been an everlasting dis- grace to the town had they failed to recognise the men who so readily responded to their country's call. (Loud applause.) He thsnked them allsincerely. Mr Posnett, who was well received, thanked Captain Timmins, Mr Taylor, and all present for the kind way in which they bad received his wife. That wan his first duty. (Applause.) His second was to ask Mrs Posnett to unveil the" roll of honour." /Loud applause.) Mrs Posnett, then accomplishea ruo task of unveiling,

div.head: THE
div.p: THE

and the "roll of honour" unfolded to the gaze of all, was greeted with enthusiastic cheering. The "Active Service Roll of Honour" is a magnificent solid oak specimen of the woodworkers art, the top being a protruding ornamental cornice,with the Prince of Wales Feathers (the badge of the Corps) as centre piece. This latter is a most exquisite and delicately carved piece of oak. Below ic runs the inscription "2nd V. 8., Cheshire Regiment, Runcorn Detachment," and at the foot of the cornice 'work runs the title panel. Three broad panels framed in nicely contrast grained oak record : "South African War 1899-1990, Sergeant F J Jeacock, Corporal W Griffiths, Lance Corporal T J Speakman, Privates A C Timmins, 13 Chadwick, L Mack, F Platt,W Parkinson, W Clark, W H Charlesworth.—lmperial Yeomanry : Troopers H Hill, P R West, W Looker, M Mellor, T Mellor, S Baokes, E Douglas H Symb• and a another name to be added is that of Private J Massey- At the foot of this record runs "God Save the King ;" and the tablet terminates with another orna- mental cornice and ecallop. The whole is the work of Messrs Garnett. Chester, and is now set in the North Wall of the Drill Hall, where it stands cut very etrik ingly in a picked ground of National Blue with pillars on either side inlet with busts nf Lord Roberts and Lord Kitchener, the work of a lace: 'inlet in Runcorn sand- stone. Mr. Posnett, in a few choicer, -inks, then referred to the pleasure it had been to go iu company with Mr. Imison soliciting subscriptions. Every where they were met in the proper spirit,:and alreadylthere was at Parr's Bank sufficient with the exception of a few pounds to meet the whole expenses. (Applause.) He endorsed Mr. Imison in his rimorks concerning the action of the workingmen of the town. (Applause.) At the outset, continued Mr Posnett, it was very unanimously decided that they were not to do anything for those who had come back, which they could not do for those who would come back. (Lend applause.) He wished to acknowledge the services of Mr Wilding,ancl the officials at the Town Hall, from each of whom he had received most willing help. (Applause.) With regard to the "roll of honour," it had been a great attraction at Chester, and when the people of that city heard it was not for themselves, but for Runcorn, a groan went up, Yet the Chester people could have one if they went about it the same way. (Applause.) Finally Mr Pornett added it was now his pleasure,as representing the town, —as representing everyone : man, woman, and child— to ask Csptain Ashton to accept that Tablet from the town, and keep it for the Volunteers for ever here. (Loud and prolonged applause). Captain Ashton, in accepting the gift, assured them it was a very great honour indeed,to be allowed to accept on behatf of the Runcorn detachment, the " roll of honour board " which bad been presented to them on behalf of the town and district of Runcorn. (Hear. hear.) It was without doubt the very greatest honour that had ever been paid to them since the V dunteer movement was first started in Runcorn; and hs was sure, he was voicing the feelings of all members of the Runcorn Detachment, when he said they were really right down proud of the 18 men by whose means the board bad been presented to them. (Loud applause). Naturally, they al: hoped that the times would be few and far between when Great Britain would have to ask for the voluntary services of her sons to help her against her enemies. (Hear, hear:) But I should such an occasion arise he could only hops and trust that Runcorn, at all events, would he, that time have young man willing to go forward to off ,r their ser- vices, and so follow thogemble example which has been', set so ably by the men whose names appeared on the "Poll of honour." (Applause.) He could assure Mr Poenett that the Runcorn Detachment would for ever prize that " roll of honour," as their greatest treasure.—(loud applause),—end he believed with Captain Timmins, all the young men of Runcorn should come forward, when. the recruiting season com- menced, and enrol themselves, se that if Occasion should at any time require it they would be in a position to make it possible to have their names inscribed on the " roll of honour," against the names of those who had already so nobly served them in South Africa, (pro- longed applause). The singing of the Notional Anthem, and three cheers for the " Citizen Soldiers " concluded an interesting and inspiring function.

div.head: Watches for Cheshire Yeomen.
div.p: Watches for Cheshire Yeomen.

On Wednesday night La.ly Lettice Grosvenor, who is staying with Countess Grosvenor at Saighton Towers, Chester, drove over to Fare lon, and at a social gather- ing presented sir local Yeomen who have just returned from the Nvar, with handsom a watches, subscribed for by residents in the neighbourhood.—Majr Lord Arthur Grosvenor, who went out to South Africa in command of one of the Cheshire companies of Imperial Yeomanry in responding to the toast of the returned Yeomen,testi- fied to the cheerful and wilting spirit in which the men underwent the hardships of cimpaigniog, and praised them for the cars they took of their horses. Return of the 3rd South Lancashire Militia Regiment. We understand that the 3rd South Lancashire Militia Rezimeat, under the command of Colonel Blackburne, are under orders to return home. rho men left War- rington early in 1930, and the ceremony of receiving the colours by the Mayor took place at the Town Hall on January 703, after a service at the Parish Church. The regiment has been engaged chiefly in guarding the lines of communication in Orange River Colony.

div.head: More Local Ambulance Men for South
div.p: More Local Ambulance Men for South
Africa.

In response to a Brigade Order recently issued. from headquarters of the St. John Ambulance Brigade. London, four more men of the Warrington Corps have volunteered for South Africa. Taey have been medically examined, also tested in nursing and first aid duties by Hon. Surgeon Reginald Smith, and proceeded on Wed- nesday to Orford Barracks to join the Royal Army Medi- cal Corps, after which they were sent to the Royal Army Medical Corps Depot, at Aldershot. to be equipped and prepared for early embarkation. Teeir names are : A Green and P Kirkham. of KauWord-road, Latchford ; El Slater, Wellfleld-street ; and W Higham, of Scott- street. Captain Waring recently in compliance with an order from headquarters, furnished a list .of names of his man who had returned from South Africa, with a view of their being supplied with the medal, the issue of which may be looked for at an early date. Under the new order married men may be accepted, and facilities will be given, when possible, for their families joining them in South Africa on the termination of hostilities, should they desire to remain in that country.

Dinner was partaken rooms, Mr. Twyrole, the pro- prietor.tar placing a substantial and well-served repast before his guests. Boating and driving absorbed the afternoon and tea was enjoyed at the "Star." After a plea iant day the party left for home at 7-25, reaching Earlestown about 9-30 The arrange- ments were carried through by Mr B.Harrison. Goon TEMPLARY. The Hope o Earlestown Lodge usual weekly f session was held in the Co-operative liall,Virargrave- road, on Monday evening, Bro Williamson, CT, presiding. After the opening services the guard announcel a surprise visit from the Pioneer Lodge, St Ilelens,•he visitors being received with honours. Bro J Pu'rishon, C T, Pioneer Lodge, took the chair, and eepressed the pleasure it gave them to be pre- sent. The following programme was submitted : Recitation, " The Dos that touch liquor shall never touch mine, Si A Punshon ; solo, "The Heavenly ; Land," Sis Atherton ; solo, " Beautiful home," Bro Walter Punehon ; reading, Bro Madril ; quintet. " Before Jehovah's awful throne " ; address by Bro Lind on, H D, on the advantages of the Order- song in Tyneside dialect." Geordie and the bairn," Bro G Punshon, for an encore giving" Home of the soul"; reading, 'Toe house with the picture hung over the door." Bro J Punshon ; chorus," Hark, ten thousand thousand voices"; recitation, " The three bidders." Sis A PanAhon ; selections on the concer- tina, Bro Leateerberrow ; Miss Watkins (Merles- town) recited in an exnellent manner" He giveth His beloved sleep. 'end being heartilfencored,recited " The Psalm of life '' ; song," The Eisteddfod," Sis Mrs Williams; recitation, "The widow's trouble and how it came,' Sis Naylor; selections on the auto- harp, Bro Chapman. A vote of thanks was heartily accorded to the vi4tors and friends on the motion of Bro Newman, seconded by Bro Woods. Sr JOHN'S CHURCH CHOIR PICNIC. The choir of St John's Church, Earlestown, and the teachers of the Sunday school, to the number of 73 left Earlestown on Saturday morning at 7-15 for their annual picnic. Rhyl was this year chosen, and when the party reached this favourite seaside haunt, the weather was gloriously fine. After a visit to the capacious Marine lake, they assembled for dinner at Lloyd's restaurant, and on the inner man being satisfied, they engaged "Char a Banes " for . a drive. Through Rhuddlan the way led to Bodelwy ddan, and here the party alighted to view the now famous Marble Church, where the choir ascending the organ loft sang ' Onward Christian Soldiers," Leaving here, the drive was continued to St. Asaph, where a visit was paid to the Cathedral. On re- turning to Rhyl, tea was partaken of at the restanrant, afterwards leaving for home at 5.51. Chester was reached at 6.20 and here there was a long wait, the party taking advantage of the in- terval by visiting the city,and King Charlie's tower. A start for Earleetowa was made at 8.50, home be- ing reached at 9.35, after a most enjoyable out, slightly marred by rain which commenceed to fall a`)aut five o'clock.

--- The Most successful of the larger West African flota - Hone recently placed before the public is says the ("Money Market Review.") the Clinton Gold Conces- sions. The Company was introduced under good aus- pices, and has a practical Board. Highly satisfactory reports have been received as to the auriferous value of the various concessions, some of which are in the heart of the Wasstu district, and are a continuation of the Tarquah series. Few West African Companies are in the strong financial condition of the Clintons Gold Con- cessions, which has a working capital of £lOO,OOO, with a further £50,000 capital in res.rve, Thiaicompany should, on receipt of reports, be in a positlon to sell portions of its enormous areas at very large profits to the shareholders. The fact tbat markets generally are inactive may account for Clintons' shares being still ob- tainable at a small premium. There should bs little risk in buying them, and a purchaser ought to realise a handsome profit.

Garden Party at the Rectory. The church workers associated with the Parish Church were by the kind invitation of the Rector and !Are Willis, entertained at a garden party in the Rectory grounds on Saturday. About 250 guests were prAent. After being welcomed by their host and hdWess, the party proceeded to the Parish Church, where an organ recital was given by Mr Darby, the organist Afterwards tea was served on the Rectory lawn, and subsequently games were commenced, but owiing to rain these were abandoned until Moqdly evening, when dancing and other amusements were kept up until a late hour. On arrival there they were joined by themembers of the Runcorn and Widnes staffi,and a bowling handicap was arranged,and after a pleasant afternoon's sport the winners were : Mr Bailey (Warrington), I; Mr Feden (Warrington), 2 ; Mr Lucas (Rainhili), 3; Mr Harnpson (Widnes), 4. The party then did justice to a capital knife-and-fork tea, provided by Mr Lucas, after which a smoking concert was held, Mr Bailey taking the chair. Songs were rendered by Mes.rs T Ashcroft, jun, W Ashcroft, Bride, Gorton (Ws -rington), and Messrs Mackley and Wynn (Wilnes); the comic element beina supplied by Mr Campbell, of Warrington. This menagerie which is one of the largest travelling shows of its kind, visited Warrington on Saturday, and many people took the opportunity of viewing the unusually comprehensive collection of wild beasts &c, exhibited. The coil -lotion em- braces over 70 different species, and the animals and birds are in the best of condition. Some rare equine curios were on view, includiog White- wing4,a beautiful horse possessing mane and tail of the combined length of 40 feet, The beasts in the cages included a number of handsome lions, tigers, bears and pumas. Some of these were put through a wonderful performance by their trainers and the unique spectacle of lious and a tiger performing in the same cage was witnessed. Among the other interesting exhibits was "General Bnytnan," the Mafeking bell-ringing ape, which so, ably assisted "B ?."and his gallant band while besieged in Mate- king. At the end of the siege he was brought to London by his owner and trainer, Trooper A T Banks. of the BSA P, and was eventually purchtved by the proprietor of the menagerie. ton Brokers Exonerated.

Before Major Lewis, at the Viridnee Police Court, on Wednesday, Owen and John APConville, marine- store dealers, were charged with stealing 117ilbs. of brass, value £5, the property of Messrs Mathie- son, chemical manufacturers. Superintendent Ke.ighley, in opening the prosecution, said the prisoners were eut on bail when they were appre- hended on a similar charge. The goods had been sold to Messrs Howards, brokers. of Warrington. Lit reply to the charge, the elder prisoner said he bought them from a man named Garkin, who, on being confronted with prisoners, denied the offence. Evidence was then. given.—Mr Knowles, who appeared for the prisoners, asked for bail.—Superiu- tendent Keighley : If bail is allowed I shall appre hend them again outside on another charge. Major Lewis remanded prisoners to the cell until Monday. —Mr Arthur Browne, who appeared for Messrs Howard, asked the Superintendent of Police to state that what part they had played in the trans- action was square and businesslike, to which he replied that the bo)lcs were kept in a proper manner, and that their dealing had been above board. They had assisted the police in every way.

Fishing Match. at Bewsey. On Saturday afternoon a novel fishing match for eels took place in the Si Helens Canal at Bewsey. It is about, 45- years since a fishing match was held here, and naturally the event created considerable interest. It was arranged by Mr Campbell, pro- prietor of the Bowling Green Inn, with the' object of ascertaining what stock of fish the canal con- tained. Over 100 competitors entered, and having drawn for positions, took up their places, twelve yards apart, on the canal bank, shortly before four o'clock. The fishing ground stretched from the Cheshire Lines Railway Arches to Buttermilk- bridge, Some of the anglers were lucky enough to make a haul within five minutes of casting in, Thd time allowed was two hours, and at the end of that period, the catches were weighed. The prizes were for the heaviest fish caught. Mr Campbell gave a copper kettle as the first prize, and six money prizes were given from the aggregate of the competitors' entrance fees. Twenty-four competi- tors caught eels, and the kettle was won by Mr II Ball, whose best fish weighed loz 14drs. The second prize was won by Mr W Hardman, with a fish of loz lldrs: and Messrs E Dark and W Harper tied for the third and fourth prices their catches weighing loz 9drs. A fish weighing loz 7drs, won the fifth prize, and Mr W Smith won the last prize his fish weighing loz 4,11.3. The arrangements for the match were carried out by Mr H Kent and a small committee. Mr John Sutcliffe, assistant borough surveyor, who; is leaving Warrington, to take up an import- ant position in London,was called before the Paving and Sewerage Committee at their meeting •on Monday evening, and the Chairman, Mr Alderman Heaton, addressing him, said that he and the com- mittee wished to thank him for the able way in which hehad performed his duties to the committee and to the Corporation, and heartily wished lkim success in his new appointment. They were very sorry to lose him, but at the same time were ;lad to hear of his success. He was sure he was spialc- ing for every member of the committee when be stated that if at any future time he or the committee could assist him in any way they would be very pleased to do so, and he could leave them with that assurance. Councillors Rogers, Burton, Piumpton, Smetharst,and the Town Clerk also bore testimony to the able way Mr 'Sutcliffe had discharged his duties. Mr Sutcliffe thanked the chairman and committee for their unexpected kind expressions towards him,and said he should:always value them. Although he was going to better himself, he should always look back with pleasure to the kind way in which the committee and every member of the Cor- poration of Warrington had treated him. A Warrington Man's Fall. A man named John Murray who resides at 23, Cartwright-street, was engaged in painting the e%- tenor of the Queen Tea Company's premises In Bridge-street at 7.15 on Tuesday evening, when he fell a considerable distance to the ground For- tunately the only injury be sustained was a cut oo the side of the face. This injury was attended tO at the Infirmary. UNDER THE CLOCK roa GOOD BOOTS.—Advt. Curious Mishap to a Warrington Cyclist. Stanley Healey, a Warrington cyclist, voils returning from Manchester on Tuesday night, whets be met with a curious accident. He was proceeding along the road skirting Lord Ellesmere's estates when a rabbit suddenly darted from the preserve close by into the roadway right in front of the cycliit. This apparition caused him to swerve,and he crashed into a farmer's lurry. The impact flung him against the Wheels of the vehicle, and he sus- tained several nasty bruises and sprained his wrist. Fortunately the lurry was going in the direction of Warrington, and the injured cyclist was carried there by it.

Proposed New Post Office. The Post Office authorities in London are endea- vouring to secure a suitable site in Warrington for a new post office. The pment building in Nankey- street, which was erected about 20 yearr, ago hag become quite inadequate for the postal business of the neighbourhood. and it is found necessary .to erect more commodious premises. The Corporator' have been approached with the object of securing a site near the present building, but no decision haS yet been come to.

LAWNMOWERS GROUND AND REPAIRED. Green Mowers always in stock--J. S. GaRLAID, Irlarnonger Bridge-street, Warrington.—Adyt. "Had' Enough of the Army." Thomas Lee was charged at Eccles on Monday with deserting from the 4th King's Liverpool Regiment. It appeared that Lee, who enlisted ill the regiment at Coins in February last, scaled the walls of Orford Barracks, Warrington, at 2 o'clock on Monday morning, and at 7 o'clock he wag captured at Peel Green, Barton, by Police-constable Barber. When arrested Lee said that be had hal enough of the army. He was remanded in custodl of the police pending the arrival of an escort. THE WARRINGTON TRAMWAY CONTRACT

--- Equipment to be made in America. The "Journal of Commerce" of New York contains the following paragraph : ,Roberc W Blackwell and Co, Limited, the British Electrical engineering concern whose local offices are in New York,has secured a con- tract from the Warrington Municipal Council calling for steel poles, brackets, trolley wires, ' insulators, etc,required for the electric traction system now being adopted by that English city. The contract, which is valued at about 25,000d01, will man that nearly all the equip- ment called for will be purchased in the United States. The contract, we un lerstaad, was accepted 001 the recommendation of the consulting electrics engineers. We believe we are correct in stating that the Council was under the impression tbo Messrs R W Blackwell and Co, Limited, was 0 British firm employing British workmen.
